#9016. Curator Christiane Paul Helped Write the History of Net Art. She’s Doing It Again with a New Survey at the Whitney.

Editor’s Note: This story is part of Newsmakers, a new ARTnews series where we interview the movers and shakers who are making change in the art world.

Rare are the times when a New York museum has turned over an entire floor to a presentation of digital art. That makes “artport: A History of Internet Art,” opening at the Whitney Museum on Saturday, an outlier in the institution’s programming—and something of a major occasion.

The titular artport is an online gallery launched in 2001 by curator Christiane Paul, who has since gone on to commission plenty of works in the intervening 25 years, by artists ranging from JODI to Mimi Ọnụọha. Officially indexed as part of the Whitney collection since 2015, artport continues to commission artists. The most recent was Jazsalyn, who, for one work staged earlier this year, proposed what she called “Black Metatheories” as means of forming something alternative to AI and called on users to respond to a range of prompts, including one that reads: “Consider blackness. How does life persist within the spectrum of impossible possibility?” Related Articles Frieze's Kristell Chadé Discusses Why the Fair Has 'Never Been About Adding Points on a Map' Newsmakers: Studio Ma's Christiana Moss on Building Museums for a Hotter, More Expensive World

Artport’s offerings live on the Whitney’s website. Generally, however, they have not been show in the Whitney’s galleries, something that will change with Paul’s exhibition opening this week, which features more than works associated with artport. The show is yet another digital art–focused exhibition from one of the great thinkers on the subject. She literally wrote the book on digital art in 2003, and is currently in the process of writing a follow-up to it.

ARTnews spoke with Paul, a curator of digital art at the Whitney, to learn more about artport’s history and how she created such an ambitious show. This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.

ARTnews: Artport was founded in 2001, but it didn’t become a part of the Whitney’s collection until 2015. More than 10 years later, what is its place at the Whitney today?

Christiane Paul: I would not say it’s changed much. The original thinking, which we kept intact, was: It’s kind of weird to lock down net art in a collection. And that is why we decided to commission the works under non-exclusive licenses. But what changed in 2015 was really that we wanted to acknowledge the artist’s status in all of this. By making it officially its own little umbrella collection within the permanent collection, all of the artists gained lifetime membership status, and are now treated the same way as collection artists—that wasn’t the case before.

Also, the works are of course more integrated into the collection database. Before, when you searched, everything was there on artport, but it did not necessarily appear in collection searches, which also became problematic when we added more physical works by some of the artists—for example, a sculpture by Auriea Harvey [whose work was commissioned by artport in 2023]—to the collection. You would find the sculpture, but not the rest of her work.

When artport commissions an artist—let’s say, for its “On the Hour” series, which stages projects on the Whitney’s website at designated times—who is the commissioner, the Whitney or artport?

The commissioner is always the Whitney Museum, and I invite artists to submit a proposal. What we don’t do is show existing work. We did a series from 2009 to 2023, “Sunrise Sunset,” that marked sunrise and sunset through a 30-second intervention into whitney.org that played on all pages. I found the format highly intriguing, because it’s so net art to disrupt, particularly an institutional website. While it was very beautiful and poetic, there also was a concern: This was sunrise and sunset, New York time only. That prompted us to change it to make it into hourly interventions.

My invitations to “On the Hour” are often based on two criteria. First of all, who are artists who can really work with that kind of seriality intervention, in terms of vignettes? I think it’s also a great way to give younger artists a chance to do something for the museum. In general, artport has always paid a lot of attention to emerging artists, but due to the format, this lends itself to being a little more experimental.

What did you look for when you started commissioning artists? How did you know an artist was good for artport?

The main goal of artport was always to show the breadth of practice in the in the online field. When artport was launched in 2001, of course, there already was a history of net art. I mean, depending on if you’re counting by accessibility to the public, the internet launched in 1993. Artistic practice in this space started around that time and really took off in the mid-’90s. So, by the time I started, there was already a backlog of the artists who were creating the language of the field: Mark Napier, Tina La Porta, Martin Wattenberg, Marek Walczak, Amy Alexander. I was rapidly moving through those people at the time. Then I was following who was doing significant work in that area.

Certainly, when you started artport, institutions had already begun paying attention to net art. Documenta X in 1997 had a net art section, and Lawrence Rinder organized a net art portion of the 2000 Whitney Biennial. You did something similar for the 2002 edition, and Rhizome partnered with the New Museum in 2003. But it seems like we’re in a very different moment now, where net art can even be the subject of major exhibitions like the artport one. What does it mean, now, to bring net art into museum walls?

I would once again say my approach has not changed that much. There’s more technological support for doing these types of shows, so the infrastructural possibilities and budget certainly did change. But since the ’90s, there has been this discussion of: “Oh, this should only be seen online.” I always thought that was such an ironic misunderstanding because online is not on your couch in your house. Online is everywhere! We’re online in the museum. People are on their phones. Everything is networked.

You’re definitely changing the context [by showing it in a museum], but it’s important to see this art in the context of other art forms, and that was very important to me. The challenge that an exhibition like this poses is: How do you make the work easily accessible within a gallery space while also maintaining its net-ness? On the one hand, it’s about not overwhelming people with dozens and dozens of screens, which we do still have in this exhibition. But we’re also changing formats quite a bit, and at the same time, we’re not sucking out what the online environment is really about.

The way I approached it with this exhibition was to use an open floor and a landscape of browser windows as a design conceit. There are floating walls held up by poles. There’s also a lot of cabling, as you can imagine. The walls or panels suggest open browser windows on which the screens are presented. They’re not segregating works into rooms—they’re all the web, where you might switch from one tab to another. Some works have been translated into more of an installation, like Andy Deck’s Screening Circle [2006], for example, which you use online, with different people contributing to it. You use your mouse to choose pixels and create an icon within this screening circle. And in the gallery, you will see it projected onto a platform with actually four tablets for input, so four people can use it simultaneously. It will switch between them and also bring in the online work.

There are also works that have components of paintings or prints, like Michael Mandiberg, for example. They did an endurance performance, Life Study [2018], where, over the course of four years, they filmed themself doing paintings of their assistants. We’re not only showing the work and its archive, but also some of the paintings.

The exhibition is titled “artport: A History of Internet Art,” which suggests that it is a history of net art, and that there are others still to be told. What is the history you’re telling?

Julia Kaganskiy puts it nicely in her essay for the catalog. There are timestamps that are demarcating the concerns, attitudes, social norms, and media environments that have shaped our collective lives. I think any type of net art that one would have picked beyond artport from the ’90s until today would somehow tell that history. Of course, the history that artport tells is a very specific one in that there are certain choices of artists, and they tell that history in a specific way, through their personal lens. If it were a completely different roster of artists, those timestamps marking these shifts would still be there, but the story would be told slightly differently.

There’s also a new performance by the artist duo Operator: the third act of their ongoing “Human Unreadable” project, begun in 2022.

Operator has, for the past four years, created the series “Human Unreadable,” which is a generative choreography on the blockchain. It’s open source, so that people can use to do their own performances. In Act I, they translated sequences that were created by the choreography into large-scale black and white images that were sold as NFTs. In Act II, collectors could reveal the movement sequence that had generated the image. From the start, the work raised the question: How much of the body survives translation into code? In Act III, we have bodies without the mediation of the screen performing the first 100 tokens choreographic sequences. It really is a multimedia theater piece that also includes spoken word, and it is really about our relationships to technological systems, the artist’s personal story, and negotiating ambition and technology in your life. And its two matinees are live streamed: I think we now have 18 partner institutions. The live stream is not simply “Oh, here is a camera that shows you what’s happening at the Whitney.” It is more of an artwork in and of itself, with moving cameras and modifications, almost a little bit more like Nam June Paik’s Good Morning, Mr. Orwell minus the technological difficulties. [Laughs.]

A lot of younger viewers who encounter this exhibition may not entirely understand everything involved in creating the early net art surveyed here—for example, the splash pages produced for artport between 2001 and 2006, which rely on a technology that is generally out of use in our current internet. How will you contextualize those pieces for viewers less familiar with them?

There were 57 splash pages—they were done monthly—and I am only showing the ones where artists created standalone projects rather than just a splash page or gate page for their work, because that kind of browsing is better done at home. The intention is to get lost in an artist’s work and website, and that would really distract from the focus of the exhibition. That being said, we are explaining the functionality of splash pages and what they were in the section text. But I hope the art of that time, and the environment of the web at the time, really translates—to me, that is actually the most significant part of the exhibition. There are these really nice connections across the floor between these early works and later ones that show you how really our attitudes towards self-representation, identity, surveillance data processing have shifted over time.

There’s an early work by Jillian McDonald that was made 20 years before deepfakes. It’s about fan culture—she inserted herself into the film Buffalo ’66 with Vincent Gallo. I have it right across from works by Tina La Porta, who did voyeur_web [2001] at a time when live casting was so popular. People would put up webcams in their homes, in their kitchens, in their bedrooms, as this kind of gesture of returning the gaze, something that people wouldn’t do anymore today. It’s a completely different attitude that gets reflected in Maya Man‘s A Realistic Day in My Life Living in New York City [2024–25], which takes this highly stylized TikTok culture of a supposedly realistic day that is completely performed and provides a counterpoint to what voyeur_web did.

The freedom that some of this early net artists had is amazing. It’s just not possible anymore, with so much of the internet became commodified, capitalized, and cleaner.

What really struck me in reviving some of the older pieces was that the first generation of net artists really used the web as material, in terms of scraping and reprocessing. The access they had, you don’t have that anymore with the corporate lockdown.

And you had to have a certain degree of technical know-how, too. I was rereading a 2015 interview you did with the artist Marisa Olson for Rhizome in which you said you were dubious that net art still existed. Do you still feel that way?

I would slightly revise my framing. [Laughs.] What I was really getting at was that in the ’90s or early 2000s, you really had a category of net artists. Those were people who really worked with the web, and that was it—that was their practice. And I think with so-called post-internet, post-digital art, this crossed over into more material form, even though the internet was still at the core of the practice. In the sense of the net artist who does work online, and that is the practice, period? I think that is much harder to find today. You still have net art, and a lot of it. I mean, Maya Man, Chia Amisola are younger artists who are really doing net art in the spirit of the online environment, but Maya also does very material works. Artists have been branching out more: They may be doing work on the web and in sculpture painting across the board. You might argue that has changed in contemporary art in general, which has become less medium-specific. But there is still net art.

#9014. 10 Signs You Might Not Really Be in Love: How to Tell the Difference

Love can feel like navigating a choose-your-own-adventure book with half the pages missing. Are you truly in love or just caught in a wave of infatuation? Sometimes, what seems like a heart-thumping romance may be a fleeting crush.

Wondering how to tell the difference? We’ve got you! Here’s a rundown of the 10 signs you’re not really in love.

Feeling a bit puzzled about your feelings for boo? That’s pretty normal. But before you start planning your future or picking out matching Halloween costumes, you may wanna make sure it’s real love and not a case of a serious crush.

Here are some signs that you may not really be in love:

Caught up in the romance novel vibe? If you’re all about the feelings of being in love rather than who’s sharing your popcorn, it might just be that you’re smitten with the idea of love itself.

Time to check if your relationship is more about the fairy tale than the real person.

Chatting with your partner shouldn’t feel as shallow as a kiddie pool. If deep talks are tougher than pulling teeth and rarer than a unicorn, it’s a red flag.

Sticking to small talk about the weather and dinner plans suggests the emotional depth for a lasting bond might be missing.

When discussions about future plans feel as far-fetched as sci-fi adventures, they may reveal underlying doubts about the relationship’s viability.

If imagining a future together feels unrealistic or undesirable, it’s time to ask yourself why. Real love plans a future; infatuation lives for the weekend.

Remember when their sock on the floor was cute? If little quirks now make you more cranky than charmed, it might mean the love goggles are off, your feelings have shifted from affection to annoyance, and the reality check has bounced.

Love is seeing imperfections and adoring them anyway.

Feeling more at ease or more ‘yourself’ when your partner isn’t around is a telling sign. If you’re secretly throwing mini-parties when they leave the room, you need to stop and think. Real-deal love means missing their chaos when they’re gone, not celebrating the silence.

Shared values are the anchor of deep, lasting relationships. If your core values clash more than a polka dot and stripes ensemble, you’re in for a rough ride, as finding common ground could be challenging!

Lasting love grows from shared beliefs and mutual respect, not from opposing battle lines.

No respect? No future. Respect is as critical to love as air is to breathing. Without mutual respect, you might just be coexisting rather than genuinely connecting.

If you no longer admire or respect each other’s opinions and choices, sustaining a healthy relationship will be difficult.

If they’re out of sight and totally out of mind, that’s not just independence — it might be indifference. When love is real, you should long for their laugh or lame jokes when they’re away. Could it be that your emotional attachment isn’t as strong as it should be for a lasting relationship?

If your best moments are consistently away from your partner, your heart might not be in it to win it. Perhaps your relationship isn’t providing enough support or happiness.

True love enriches your life and doesn’t play second fiddle to your social circle. It’s time to evaluate where your emotional energy is invested.

Still window shopping while you’re supposedly locked down? It’s a sign you might not be all in. A love that lasts doesn’t keep a backup catalog — it’s too busy loving what it already has.

Knowing why you’re still scanning for alternatives can help you address what might be missing or unfulfilled in your relationship.

Are you genuinely in love or just in love with being in love? If you’re secretly thrilled when they’re not around, stuck in surface-level chit-chat, or dreading deep-future talks, these are cosmic signs that it’s rethink o’clock.

Don’t ignore the signals — tuning in now can save you heartache later and lead you toward a love that genuinely fulfills you.

Last medically reviewed on June 26, 2024

Manchester-based design and creative festival Motion North has announced the line up for Motion North 2027, which is to be held on 10th and 11th March at Freight Island, Manchester.

The two day festival is known as the industry event for international big name speakers, but with an intimate feel. Packed with over 20 speakers across three stages, and creative workshops to get stuck into, the festival hosts a schedule of content that promises diversity of thought and creative excellence. The aim of the talks are to inspire and challenge the next generation of creatives, and offer fresh insight for those working in the creative industries.

Highlights of the speaker line up from the world of motion design, animation, branding and design includes industry leaders in high end 3D product and brand films, Found, multi award winning artist Lucas Zanotto who blends his product design roots with playful artistry; infamous illustration and animation maestros, Nice Shit,; Emmy award winning animation director, Margherita Premuroso and Oscar winning VFX studio DNEG.

The current line up is here, with more speakers to be announced in the run up to the festival.

Excitingly, in addition to the talks, is a new place to hang out – The Marketplace: a curated showcase where independent artists have been invited to present and sell their unique crafts, graphic prints and books. In addition to this, there will also be a programme of social mixers, including an event hosted by Creative Brunch, with more announcements to come.

Established in Manchester in 2010 as a space for the creative community to meet and share ideas and experiences, Motion North is brought to the creative community by MightyGiant studio, which aims to champion the industry and bring a leading professional event to the city of Manchester.

#9012. After Exile, Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara’s Prison Drawings Arrive in New York

In one of Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara’s prison drawings, swans skim a swimming pool inside a cell. In another, a clownish figure peers over the prison wall, perched with apparent ease on barbed wire. The Cuban artist and leader of the San Isidro Movement made thousands of such works in Guanajay, a maximum-security prison outside Havana, where he served time after his arrest on July 11, 2021, amid anti-government protests across the island. His release this year, after international outcry over creative freedom, was contingent on exile to the United States. A small selection of those works makes up “Tocar el cielo,” their first public showing, now at the New York gallery Foreign & Domestic (curated by Alexander Meurice, and on view through December 13). Related Articles After Days of Uncertainty, Cuban Artist Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara Arrives in Miami Jailed Dissident Artist Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara Pens Appeal to 'People of Conscience' On Two-Year Anniversary of Arrest: 'Every Young Cuban Is a Political Prisoner'

Art that emerges from incarceration tends to speak first in material, with scarcity making resourcefulness something like a protagonist. Otero Alcántara recounted drawing on drink cartons and cigarette packs, and smuggling in colored ink that ended up on other prisoners’ skin, when bodies were canvas enough. Who gets to make art inside, and who can get supplies to them, comes with its own politics. But he describes his five years in prison as one long performance, an “involuntary artistic gesture,” and the show reflects rather than transcribes the specifics of injustice. It’s an oblique testimony to how, bereft of sky or savior, the mind can slip its confines.

ARTnews spoke with Otero Alcántara via email about his experience making art in prison, and settling into his second life in Miami. The following conversation has been translated from Spanish and condensed for publication.

ARTnews: How is your spirit these days? What has surprised you most about settling into life here?

Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara: I think it’s been a shock. It’s unsettling, and it scares me a little.

People outside Cuba could connect with my work, but it grew out of life in the neighborhood, out of my connection with the people there. Above all, it came from knowing that neighborhood called Cuba, that neighborhood called Havana, where I was like a fish in water.

In New York, I’m getting to know other ways of thinking, other ways of doing things. I’m learning how art relates to people here and how people relate to art. There’s the language barrier, too. In my own practice, I want art to disappear into the social fabric, into people’s lives. I want it to have a real effect on the person walking down the street.

I feel like an embryo, like I’m learning from scratch how art and people relate to one another. So yes, it scares me. I’d call it a difficult process, but it’s a living process.

Can you tell me about making art in prison? How did you get supplies, and when did you work? What did materials typically cost you?

I started making art the moment I set foot in prison. They put me in a punishment cell, and I spent about two or three months there. Before prison, I was detained more than 50 times in three years. Even if they only held me for two or three days, I always made something in the cell. At first, I didn’t have the materials I had later. When I finished a drink my family had brought me, I’d keep the carton and draw on it. I used cigarette packs too. I’d stitch them together to make a surface I could draw on.

Once the materials from home ran out, my friends sent me more. When I called, all those friends of mine—Yanelys Núñez, Claudia Genlui, Coco Fusco, Camila Lobón, Anamely Ramos—picked up the phone. That was an act of resistance and an act of friendship. They took money they could have spent on food or on things they needed and used it to send me good art supplies, really good ones, all the way to Cuba, into the prison where I was being held.

That’s what I mean by cultural resistance. For my friends, it meant keeping the art alive and keeping the artist alive. They taught me how good it is to have a friend, and how good it is to be one.

Can you tell me about the recurring figure in the prison cell works? You’ve depicted him as a clown. Who does he represent? Who, or what, is the joke?

The clown keeps coming back in my work. When I look back at everything I made in prison, from beginning to end, I can see that the figures in those first drawings and paintings really were clowns. Over time, all that was left of the clown was the nose and traces of this strange makeup that gradually broke down. The colors started to bleed into one another. I feel that had something to do with how I was changing, how I was growing older in prison. At one point, even the paper tears. I tear it. I don’t know if it was hatred, if I was channeling hatred through my hands, or frustration. I don’t know why it was a clown.

As for the question about the joke, I remember being on hunger strike once, in a group of prisoners that included several men who’d protested on July 11. We’d become friends in there. They were getting sentences of ten years, eight years, five years. It literally seemed like a joke.

To me, the whole thing felt like a circus, like watching a show, only this show had real consequences for people’s lives. So if there’s a joke in it, if there’s an irony, that’s where I see it. They put up this whole circus tent. What happens under it affects so many people’s lives, and none of it makes any sense.What was it like to go years without seeing your whole reflection?

In prison, there was a tiny mirror. Mirrors are prized possessions in there. You hold yours out and someone in another cell, maybe three or six feet away, holds his out too. And there, in that little piece of mirror, you can see the other man’s face. You can see when a guard is coming.

If your mirror is only four inches across, all you ever see of yourself is a piece of your face. You never see your whole body. You go into prison looking one way and come out looking another. The first time I stood in front of a full-length mirror again, it was like coming back to see someone and finding myself face to face with a new person.

I think that found its way into my work. I have a series of self-portraits where my features start to disappear. They’re smudges, scratches, moods. Most of the work I made in prison was like that. I painted states of mind.

The only portraits that came close to being realistic were the ones I made of my friends. It was all about memory. I wanted to keep existing in my friends’ minds, and I wanted to remember them, too.Two of your works involve faith: a cross, and beside it a pile of idols sinking into an abyss. What is the relationship between your art and faith?

My art has a lot to do with faith and religion. For me, those are two different things. Both are tied to being Cuban. And for as long as I can remember, people have had faith that the system would fall, that the dictatorship would come to an end, that life would get better.

In Cuba, you have very little power to change the reality you live in. There’s no democracy, and the system makes you feel like you can’t fend for yourself. On the island, you’re always waiting for somebody on the outside to save you. And by “save you,” I mean a cousin or a brother sending you money. It’s like having faith in a god who lives somewhere out there, some kind of extraterrestrial being who’s going to keep you going on the island. You put your faith in finding a girlfriend or a boyfriend who has money, or in a foreigner coming along, marrying you and taking you away. The system is so rigid that you have very little room to change your own circumstances.

Before prison, I made performances that drew on images of the Virgin Mary and the saints. What interests me is how these objects change the way people behave, how they shape a culture, and how those in power use them to manipulate people.

Prison is maybe one of the last places where you lose whatever say you still had over your own life. Your future is in the hands of a prosecutor or whoever else gets to decide. It’s like living in a jungle where a lion decides which animal it wants to eat that day, and you pray it won’t be you.

Confinement also brings you face-to-face with yourself. You get in touch with something more visceral in yourself, something more animal. And all you’re left with is the faith that tomorrow might be better.

That reminds me of a story about a friend of mine in prison. He’d been waiting a year or so for his trial, and he was getting desperate. Nothing had been proven against him.

One day he used the five minutes a week they gave him on the phone to call his lawyer. He said, “Hey, tell me something. Any news?”

His lawyer said, “Don’t worry. Last night I dreamed they were going to let you go.”

In another work, a maze fills the cell. Is it a way out or another kind of trap?

I think the labyrinth has to do with how you feel in prison. When you’re in prison, you really have no way out. But there’s also the question of what you can do with that one small space. You have to turn it into your own amusement park. For me, the labyrinth is about the thousand ways you have to reinvent one space to survive in it.

There’s also something about getting lost so you can find yourself again, and finding yourself only to get lost again. As time goes by, you get tangled up in nostalgia, in sadness, in forgetting. You feel whole places in your mind starting to disappear, and you find yourself holding on to the memory of them.

Your practice is so community-driven. How did you keep that part of yourself alive in solitary?

The place where I lived was called Pasillo 20, Corridor 20. It was in the maximum-security section at Guanajay, cut off from most of the other prisoners. For five years, I lived among about 20 men.

Some of the men painted or drew. I started what I called the San Isidro Grants. For two or three months, as long as my money lasted, I gave some money to men who painted and bought them materials so they could keep painting. I brought in art history books and gave them away.

I also made work outside the prison while I was still inside. One piece that mattered a lot to me was Momento Cero, which I made with Coco Fusco. People counted down the days I had left in prison. There was also Fe de vida. During the Havana Biennial, we invited curators and artists to come to visit me in prison. Reaching out to people outside was connected to what I was doing with the men I lived with, finding ways to make room for community, kindness and love in a place that was so violent.

You arrived in the United States at a moment when artists here are facing censorship and funding cuts on a scale I haven’t seen in my lifetime. What has it been like to land in this context?

First of all, I feel like I haven’t quite landed here yet. I mean that physically, in my body, but also in my thinking and how I see things as an artist. What I can say is that the little I’ve seen and heard here doesn’t come close to the lack of freedom in Cuba.

Now I’ve come to a country I hope will be a place of passage for me. When you speak from New York, your words carry more legitimacy than if you’re speaking from, say, Havana or Haiti. I don’t know why the world gives that so much weight. Well, yes, I do know why.

Coming here, I can see that this country is going through a transition, a crisis. There’s conflict in the relationships between institutions, art, and artists. I think this is a moment when artists have to take responsibility. We can use art to resist, to change things, and to put forward a vision of a better world.

Do you see any parallels between what you experienced in Cuba and what’s happening here, or do you see them as fundamentally different?

The danger in drawing a parallel is that someone can always say, “Look what happens to people in Cuba. That doesn’t happen to you here. You’ve got me to thank for that, so you have to do what I say.” That’s where populism comes in. If you understand which freedoms an American artist enjoys and what artists elsewhere have to live without, you have a starting point. You can defend the ground you’ve gained and recognize when someone is using those freedoms to blackmail you.

We need to keep those differences in view. That’s how we recognize what we’ve already won as a nation and keep fighting for the freedoms we still need.

How have Cubans on the island and in the diaspora responded to the politics of your release and to your ability to keep making art in prison?

I think my art and the art of my generation, the work of the San Isidro Movement and others, have had an impact on Cuba, both on the island and in the diaspora. It’s only been five years since July 11, 2021, and people already recognize the part that my work, and the art we made together in San Isidro, played in the spirit of rebellion that emerged in 2018, 2019, 2020 and 2021.

For me, those five years in prison are one big work of art, one long performance. I call it “an involuntary artistic gesture.” The dictatorship acts on my body against my will, and what it does to me provokes an aesthetic response in other people.

The other thing that matters is social media and everything that played out there when I arrived in the United States. What struck me was how it exposed some bad habits that have taken hold in the way Cubans use social media. I’m talking about people acting irresponsibly. Some influencers have learned how to make money on YouTube, Facebook and Instagram. Controversy brings in viewers, and viewers bring in money.

What matters most to me is what I’ve experienced walking the streets of Miami. From 99 percent of the people I’ve met, if not 100 percent, what I’ve felt is affection. I’ve felt love.

When you think about what art is for and what an artist owes the world, has your view changed since prison?

I think art is one of the tools we have as human beings to transform society and culture. And when I say culture, I mean it in the broadest sense, right down to the way we behave. Those in power know what art can do. They use it when it serves their interests. When it doesn’t, they go after it. They try to put art itself in prison.

Art is one of the teeth on the gear that keeps society moving. And the artist is the one who thinks, who proposes something, who puts their own body on the line. So, I think the artist bears the greatest responsibility.

An artist’s responsibility extends to humanity as a whole. There’s a commitment to humanism there: understanding that you have power and, more than that, a responsibility. Because if you don’t use your art to help people, someone else will use it for purposes that don’t help them.

When you picture your studio, or your next show, a year from now, what do you see?

A year from now, I’d love the work I brought out of Guanajay to have found homes in archives, museums and private collections. I want someone standing there to get a sense of what one human being lived through in confinement. I was a Cuban in prison. I was also a human being locked up. Someone in a prison anywhere in the world could go through what I went through, you know? For my studio, what I want is room to work and room to try things. There are sculptures I want to propose, ideas I couldn’t develop in Cuba because of the repression.

I also hope I’ll have helped more Americans understand something about Cuba. Our two peoples are so close, yet there’s still a romantic view of Cuba here, and that has consequences for us Cubans. Fidel Castro was a dictator. We’ve lived under a dictatorship for more than 60 years.

More than anything, I’d like people in the arts here to understand our work and make room for it in the stories and images that are part of everyday American life. What happens on that island finds echoes in so many other places.

#9011. BIG reveals "modular blueprint" for Refugee City in Uganda

Architecture studio BIG has unveiled plans for Refugee City, a masterplan that reimagines the Bidi Bidi refugee settlement in Uganda as an economic hub.

Developed by BIG in collaboration with social enterprise To.org, the masterplan proposes essential civic infrastructure such as housing, schools and markets for the largest refugee settlement in Africa, home to around 250,000 displaced people.

The initiative was conceptualised as an alternative to short-term aid and charity-led approaches to refugee settlements, providing a “resilient economic model” that empowers displaced communities.

“If the average stay in refugee camps is around two decades, then the term temporary cannot be said to suffice,” said studio founder Bjarke Ingels.

“If we start thinking of cities rather than camps, then charity becomes investments into the future, and if companies can be incentivised to locate their production in refugee cities, then the refugees can be given economic opportunities that they currently long for.”

If completed, the project would sit alongside an existing performing arts centre completed on the site in 2024.

The masterplan is designed by BIG to be “scalable and modular” to facilitate its implementation in other locations.

“We have attempted to design a scalable, phaseable, modular blueprint for a new way to accommodate the global flow of refugees,” Ingels said.

In a bid to allow the city to grow organically, the proposal takes a “fractal approach” – beginning with the establishment of housing units before expanding to neighbourhoods and eventually districts over several years.

The first phase of the project comprises a prototype single-family housing unit, which is currently being built on the site. Its modular structure was designed to improve existing shelter typologies, while also drawing on local buildings.

Once complete, the unit will function as an operational guesthouse to accommodate international investors and future collaborators on the site.

“The prototype base unit is inspired by local vernacular settlements where homes grow as a sequence of rooms around shared spaces,” To.org co-founder Nachson Mimran told Dezeen.

Renders of the city reveal designs for a commercial street lined with markets and built from local materials such as brick and bamboo.

The Bidi Bidi settlement in Uganda was chosen as the site for the inaugural Refugee City because of the country’s 2006 Refugee Act, which grants refugees the right to work and start businesses, freedom of movement, and to acquire agricultural plots within integrated rural settlements.

“There are very few nations offering this unique combination which makes Uganda the ideal location for the inaugural Refugee City,” Mimran said.

The realisation of the full-scale masterplan in Bidi Bidi is dependent on capital investment, while any future initiatives will require host-nation governments to be willing to grant flexibility and legal work rights to refugees.

#9010. Say What? 7 Tips to Unclog Your Blocked Ears

Earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure might be behind your clogged ears. There are many easy ways to get relief at home.

Whether it’s from a cold, allergies, or changes in air pressure, blocked ears can disrupt your day-to-day activities and even cause discomfort. Thankfully, there are several effective methods to help unclog your ears and restore your hearing. Listen up!

Why are my ears clogged?

Clogging can happen either on the inside or the outside of your eardrum. Here are the most common ways your ears can get blocked:

  • Earwax in the outer ear helps prevent particles and excess water from entering the middle ear. However, if earwax builds up too much outside the eardrum, it can cause a blockage.
  • If you’ve been swimming recently, some water might be stuck in your ear canal, pushing against your eardrum. When that water hangs around too long, it can lead to a swimmer’s ear, an outer ear infection.
  • Sinus infections, ear infections, and Eustachian tube dysfunction can pressure your eardrum’s inner side.
  • Allergies can cause uncomfortable inflammation and congestion in your ears. Your sinuses, throat, and ears are connected, so when you feel stuffed up and sniffly, your inner ear feels the pain too.
  • Changes in air pressure, like when you fly, can cause uncomfortable ear pressure.

Best clogged ear remedies

1. Pop and unclog

The easiest way to unclog your ears is by “popping” them. Just pinch your nose shut, seal your lips, and gently blow. This simple technique, known as the Valsalva maneuver, won’t clear earwax or fluid but is a common trick people use on planes.

2. Swallow, yawn, or chew

The Eustachian tubes connect your middle ear to the back of your throat. They briefly open when you swallow, yawn, or chew. Altitude changes can cause these tubes to close, but chewing gum or yawning can help reopen them. Alternatively, you can try the Toynbee maneuver, where you hold your nose and swallow.

3. Ear drops

Over-the-counter (OTC) ear drops can soften and dissolve excess earwax. If you prefer a DIY approach, warm a small amount of mineral oil and use an eye dropper to apply a few drops into your ear for a few minutes.

Pro tip: Baby oil or olive oil can also be used, but make sure it’s not too hot. Additionally, diluted hydrogen peroxide drops can be helpful.

4. Warmth and gravity

To loosen up clogged earwax, use a warm, damp washcloth as a compress. Lie down with the clogged ear facing down against the heated washcloth. Gravity and heat will help the earwax move along more easily.

5. Hit the steam room

Steam can help drain sinuses and alleviate pressure in your inner ear. Close the bathroom door, let the hot shower run for a while, and then luxuriate with deep, cleansing breaths. 

6. Take allergy medication

Because your throat, sinuses, and ears are interconnected, any sickness affecting your sinuses or throat can also impact your ears.

Over-the-counter antihistamines, decongestants, or nasal sprays can relieve sniffles, coughs, and ear discomfort.

7. Rinse away the gunk

Rinsing your nasal passages with a medication-free saline solution can help reduce congestion and clear out mucus that might be causing ear blockage. You can also consider investing in a nasal irrigation system for more thorough mucus clearing.

When to see your doctor

Have you been unable to unclog your ears for a few days, or are you experiencing severe pain, fever, dizziness, hearing loss, fluid discharge, or unusual odor? If so, it’s crucial to contact your healthcare provider promptly. These symptoms may indicate an infection that needs medical attention.

What not to do when you have clogged ears

  • Cotton swabs: Q-tips and other cotton swabs to remove earwax can push it further into your ear canal, so don’t do it. 
  • Candling: Ear candles might seem like a fun party trick, but there’s no science to prove they work, and they’ve been shown to cause injuries.
  • Sprays: Decongestant nasal sprays can be helpful, but using them too long can lead to rebound congestion.
  • Drying solutions: A few drops of rubbing alcohol or a mixture of one part vinegar and one part alcohol can help dry out the ears when you have a swimmer’s ear. However, doing this regularly can lead to irritation.

Takeaway

Clogged ears are often caused by earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure. You can use over-the-counter or DIY ear drops, irrigation kits, or warm compresses to unblock your ears. Antihistamines or nasal sprays can also help relieve clogs caused by allergies.

PSA: Consult a healthcare provider if your blocked ears are painful or at-home remedies don’t work.

#9009. British Museums Are Experiencing a ‘Bayeux Bounce’ in Attendance, Thanks to Replicas of the Tapestry

The Bayeux Tapestry is the gift that keeps on giving. UK museums such as Reading Museum and the Great North Museum: Hancock are experiencing a “Bayeux bounce,” according to the Museums Association.

Replicas of the scroll-like panel of linen cloth, which measures at 230 feet long and is populated with 58 scenes, are driving visitors to museums other than the British Museum, where the tapestry is on loan until July next year. Tickets to the British Museum’s presentation have been sold out numerous times. Related Articles Bayeux Tapestry Display to Change Upon Return to Normandy Next Year George Osborne Personally Helped Secure Controversial $6.6 M. British Museum Sponsorship, Emails Show

Reading Museum’s museum manager, Matthew Williams, said that the museum’s Victorian replica of the Bayeux Tapestry has driven a 74 percent increase in footfall since October, with 16,693 visitors. The tapestry at Reading Museum is free to visit, and photography is allowed, unlike at the British Museum, where the tapestry is ticketed at £33 and photography is banned in order to control the long queues.

“We have trained more staff to deliver our public tours and recruited more welcome volunteers to help us manage the crowds, especially at weekends and school holidays,” said Williams. “We have made sure to keep our website updated to manage expectations and to clearly show when the [replica] Bayeux Tapestry is closed for booked tours or when it will be busy, to avoid disappointment.”

The Bayeux Tapestry replica has resulted in optimistic numbers for the museum, with tours booked until June 2027, the cafe’s income up by 46 percent, donations increased by 83 percent, and shop sales soaring by 93 percent.

The copy of the Bayeux Tapestry at the Great North Museum: Hancock is on display until January 17, 2027, and is made out of paper, stretching approximately 16 feet longer than the original. The museum has experienced a 23 percent increase in visitors this October, with 3,107 more visitors than last year, while donations have climbed 30 percent, retail up 13 percent and the cafe hopping by 11 percent.

Other museums are taking advantage of the Bayeux Tapestry replica. The Nicholson Institute in Staffordshire will display its own copy from January 12 to March 31, 2027.

#9008. Polestar Formula 2030 concept car "screams performance"

Swedish electric-vehicle brand Polestar has unveiled the Formula 2030 concept car featuring interchangeable, customisable dashboard buttons.

The first Polestar concept created under the direction of head of design Philipp Römers, the Formula 2030 is intended to herald the design direction of the company’s production cars in the coming years.

It takes the form of a low-slung sports car with proportions that Römers said “scream performance”.

With signature “Dual Blade” headlights, the front of the car previews the face of the next-generation Polestar 2, a saloon scheduled to launch in 2027.

Meanwhile, the tail of the Formula 2030 mirrors the upcoming Polestar 7 crossover SUV, moving away from the continuous rear lightbar that has become widespread among electric cars in favour of separate “Single Blade” lights.

Unlike Polestar’s most recently released production vehicles, the Polestar 4 and Polestar 5, the Formula 2030 also has a conventional rear windscreen.

“Design should always reflect the values and mission of a brand and that is exactly what we did with Polestar Formula 2030 concept,” said Römers, who joined Polestar from Audi in January 2025.

“It is a physical embodiment of how we apply Polestar’s core values of design, performance and sustainability to the next production cars.”

At 1.35 metres tall, 4.68 metres long and 2.02 metres wide, the Formula 2030 has a very low roofline but a broad stance.

Its styling was intended to project power, with a long bonnet, wraparound windscreen, short overhangs, muscular haunches and substantial 22-inch wheels.

Other sporty design elements include a deep front splitter and a single vertical windscreen wiper.

The Formula 2030 showcases a newly developed paint colour called Nitrogen, with accents of gold dotted throughout the car.

Inside, the design echoes efforts in recent concept cars from other carmakers to emphasise the driving experience.

The cockpit features a curved screen band mounted above the steering wheel, presenting information to the driver.

Another screen is integrated into the centre console, which slopes gently up to the dashboard.

A sliding “drive mode selector” on the centre console would allow the car to alternate between three modes – Performance, Normal and Autonomous – changing the angle of the central screen, seating and steering wheel to allow for a more passive or active driving position.

The Formula 2030 embraces a wider trend in car design back towards incorporating physical buttons, rather than only touchscreens.

Also occupying the central console is an interface of eight large mechanical controls. These can be configured to the user’s preferences, with choices between different types of buttons and switches capable of being programmed for specific functions.

In a modest nod to sustainability, the seat backs are made from a bio-based composite combining European flax and bio-based polypropylene, while the insides of the doors are made from a single material in order to be recyclable.

Headquartered in Gothenburg, Polestar has emphasised design and sustainability since it was spun out of Volvo as a premium EV brand in 2017.

Amid heavy financial losses, it has increased its production of SUVs, which tend to be popular with consumers and deliver higher profit margins. SUVs or SUV-adjacent cars now account for three of the five models in its lineup.

SUVs are often associated with a greater environmental impact than other types of cars, but Polestar denies watering down its ambitions on sustainability.

According to its most recent sustainability report, published in April, the company is ahead of schedule on a target to halve greenhouse-gas emissions per vehicle sold between 2020 and 2030.

It is the only car brand that publishes life-cycle carbon assessments for all its models. Assessments for the upcoming Polestar 2 and Polestar 7 have not yet been calculated.

“Learnings from the cars we have already produced will be channelled into the new cars to bring the CO2e figures in as low as possible,” a spokesperson told Dezeen.

In 2021, Polestar announced a project to produce a “truly climate-neutral car” by 2030. Earlier this year, it pushed this target back to 2035 owing to the “scale and complexity of the challenge”.

Other concept cars recently covered on Dezeen include the flying Tesla Roadster and a Fiat that transforms from an SUV into a pickup truck.

#9007. Are Tangerines Good for You? 5 Health Benefits You Might Love

Tangerines are not just tasty — they’re a powerhouse of nutrients. Packed with tangy flavor and vibrant orange color, these citrus delights offer a host of health benefits. From boosting your immune system to rejuvenating your skin, tangerines are nutrient-rich allies for your well-being. Let’s delve into their nutritional profile and discover why they’re a smart addition to your diet.

Tangerines are nutritional powerhouses. Here’s what each of these little champs pack under their orange belts:

Tangerines are teeny cousins of the orange but with a thinner, easier-to-peel skin. They boast a sweet and juicy flavor and pack a ton of vitamins, particularly vitamin C, as well as minerals like potassium, antioxidants, and dietary fiber.

These tiny bursts of sunshine have many benefits that can significantly enhance your health. Here’s why you might want to make tangerines a regular part of your diet:

Tangerines are loaded with vitamin C, turning them into tiny, tasty guardians for your health. This crucial vitamin supercharges your immune system by enhancing the function and effectiveness of white blood cells, which are essential for fighting off pathogens and infections. By improving the activity and response of these cells, vitamin C helps your body combat a wide range of infections more effectively.

Therefore, regular consumption of these mini-oranges satisfies your taste buds and boosts your body’s defense mechanisms — a win-win!

Want that glow? Tangerines have got you covered. They’re high in potassium, a real game-changer for regulating hydration and balancing fluid levels in your skin cells. This essential mineral keeps your skin cells plump and hydrated, warding off pesky, dry, dull patches.

Plus, potassium supports the removal of toxins and wastes, which means clearer, more radiant skin.

Tangerines are also a fantastic source of vitamin A, which strengthens the outer layer of your skin, smoothing out wrinkles and reducing fine lines. Along with vitamin C, it’s a potent antioxidant, protecting your skin from the damaging and aging effects of free radicals.

Are you having tummy troubles? Tangerines can help with a fiber boost that keeps things moving smoothly along your digestive tract.

These zesty little superheroes are your gut’s new best friends. They’re loaded with fiber that bulks up and softens things down there, making your bathroom visits smooth and speedy. This fruity fix helps manage everything from irregular pit stops to those bloated bleurgh days.

Fiber also balances your gut flora, promoting a healthy microbial environment in your intestines. This balance is crucial for optimal digestion, nutrient absorption, and immune function.

So, grab a tangerine to remedy your belly blues next time your gut feels out of whack.

Tangerines are a dynamo when it comes to battling serious health baddies like cancer and heart disease. These little orange wonders are loaded with flavonoids, natural compounds that help with heart health and cancer prevention.

Flavonoids help relax the blood vessels, lowering blood pressure levels and reducing the strain on your heart. This helps keep your ticker ticking smoothly and reduces the risk of cardiovascular diseases like heart attacks and strokes.

But wait, there’s more! When it comes to cancer, flavonoids mess with the bad guys — cancer cells — stopping them from multiplying and spreading their nonsense around your body.

Keep your peepers sharp with a dose of vitamin A from tangerines. This essential nutrient and compounds like beta-carotene shield your eyes from age-related issues and support healthy vision. It plays a key role in creating rhodopsin, a protein in your eyes that allows you to see in low-light conditions.

Munching on tangerines helps keep your night vision in superhero shape and supports overall eye function, keeping your peepers sharp and responsive.

Furthermore, tangerines contain other essential eye health nutrients, like lutein and zeaxanthin. These antioxidants are found in high concentrations in the retina, where they help filter blue light and prevent oxidative damage, further protecting the eyes from conditions like cataracts.

Sure, tangerines are delish and make your taste buds do a happy dance, but they’re also packed with nutrients that can seriously amp up your well-being.

From giving your immune system a high-five to keeping your heart beating like a healthy drum, tangerines are basically wellness wrapped in a bright orange peel. So, go grab one and make it your main squeeze!

#9006. Volcanoes! Floods! The Apocalypse! All Appear in a Rare $1.3 M. German Manuscript Coming to Christie’s

Natural disasters, cosmic phenomena, and Biblical tales of destruction have long fascinated humankind and sometimes have been thought to convey messages from above. Christie’s London will offer a prominent example of a 16th-century German manuscript with 167 miniature renditions of phenomena such as comets, monsters, and the end of the world.

In the The Book of Miracles, also known as the Augsburger Wunderzeichenbuch, which bears an estimate of £700,000–£1 million (about $923,000–$1.3 million), readers see bloodred moons, fiery comets, floods, cities smashed by earthquakes, swarms of giant locusts, volcanic eruptions, dragons, and “monstrous births.” It comes to the auction block as part of Christie’s classic week sale of valuable books and manuscripts in London on December 10. The house bills it as “one of the most remarkable surviving picture chronicles” of its century. Related Articles Whitney Museum Is Selling a de Kooning Painting Just Three Years After Receiving It Christie's Posts Highest Watch Total Ever and Sells Bulgari Pink Diamond for $14 M.

The volume comes from the holdings of the widely respected American collector Mickey Cartin. Christie’s is offering up to $8 million worth of selections from his collection, ranging from Netherlandish painting to contemporary art and, of course, rare books. Upward of 80 objects will be spread over more than 10 auctions in London, Paris, and New York, from this November until July 2027.

The Book of Miracles was completed in the city of Augsburg around 1552. Its geographical origins are known because some of the captions refer to events “here in Augsburg,” and the paper bears watermarks associated with that city and time period. The makers are thought to be Hans Burgkmair the Younger, Heinrich Vogtherr the Younger, and their respective workshops. Its imagery, says the auction house, draws on the work of some of the best-known artists of the German Renaissance, such as Albrecht Dürer and Hans Holbein the Younger.

The book begins with the Creation described in the Christian Bible and moves chronologically through other events in that book as well as ancient and medieval history, and finally, the Apocalypse. Events that were relatively newsy at the time appear, including a celestial phenomenon observed from Augsburg in 1541 and a hailstorm in Dordrecht in 1552.

The book traces back to a private collection in Bavaria. Munich bookseller and auctioneer Hugo Ruef, describing it as coming from the library of a small South German Baroque castle, sold it in 2008 for €127,500 ($140,305 at today’s rate of exchange). By 2010, it was with London dealer James Faber, who specializes in European drawings, and then it went to Cartin.

“The Book of Miracles is an extraordinary window onto the Renaissance imagination,” said Eugenio Donadoni, Christie’s international specialist in medieval and Renaissance manuscripts, in press materials. “Its 167 miniatures capture a world fascinated by signs, wonders and unexplained phenomena, bringing together comets, eclipses, floods, monstrous births and visions of the Apocalypse. What makes the manuscript particularly compelling is the way it sits between observation and belief: these images record real events and natural phenomena, while also revealing how people in the 16th century sought to understand what they were seeing and what these extraordinary occurrences might signify.”

As the New York Review of Books noted in 2014, on the occasion of a new facsimile printing by Taschen, the 16th-century book came as part of a “boom” in compendia of miracles that grew out of a new focus on reading the Bible, and wrote that in it, “One astonishing, delicious, supersaturated picture follows another.” Apollo fittingly described the book as “a revelation,” notes Taschen.

#9005. Perforated brick walls envelop giant market in Kinshasa by Think Tank Architecture

Photography by Martin Argyroglo excluding top photo by Ville Kinshasa & SZTC

French studio Think Tank Architecture has created a market in the capital of the Democratic Republic of Congo, with space for 20,000 vendors across its geometric brick-and-concrete structure.

Named Zando Central Market, the building replaces a historic market on the same site in Kinshasa that was demolished after insufficient maintenance and an overwhelming number of vendors left it unfit for purpose.

Think Tank Architecture was brought in to design the replacement market after the original building had already been torn down. The studio used this as an opportunity to completely reimagine the role and function of the market, while taking visual cues from the original building and others like it in the city.

Alongside an increased number of vendor stalls, the 82,000-square-metre replacement incorporates storage space, a fire station, a police station, a medical centre, a vet’s, offices and a food court.

“The new market is on the same site as the ancient one, on the 3.7-hectare plot,” Think Tank Architecture told Dezeen.

“However, the building’s footprint has been totally redefined, taking into consideration the scale of the program and the urban context,” it continued.

“We wanted it to be an African market, and not an interpretation of it. Our comprehension comes from academic, historic and architectural research, dialogue with the client and then visits to other markets in Kinshasa.”

Zando Central Market has a rectangular plan measuring 245 metres in length and 150 metres in width. It contains 650 shops with space for 20,000 vendors, which is “more than 5 times its original capacity”, according to the studio.

At its heart is the central covered market, spanning two double-height levels, with three large entrances and outward views used to orient visitors.

It is surrounded by a three-storey building containing the other facilities. Landscaped patios punctuate the plan, carving out space for public squares and informal markets to take place.

“It’s an important part of our approach to keep the building open to the public, including the more modest,” said Think Tank Architecture.

The material palette for the project comprises brick and concrete, chosen to be in keeping with the local context and skills of the region’s construction workers. Demolition waste from the original market was used in the substructure.

“We are quite happy to say that this project reactivated three terracotta factories within a 60-kilometre distance from the market,” reflected the studio.

It uses a mushroom-slab structural system, in which the columns flare at their top, referencing the original market’s design.

Meanwhile, the perforated brick facades were designed to facilitate natural ventilation and provide shade from the sun.

In tandem with the thermal mass from the concrete, this helps cool the building, minimising the need for technical cooling equipment and keeping project costs low.

Interior finishes were also kept deliberately simple for cost reasons. However, the perforations of the facades help add flourish, evoking moucharabiehs – a type of projecting oriel window enclosed with wooden latticework, typically seen in traditional Islamic architecture.

Zando Central Market is on the eight-strong shortlist for the civic project category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards, alongside projects including Sydney Fish Market by 3XN and TCC DAKA Renewable Resource Recycling Center by KPF.

It is yet to officially open, as the second phase of the project – involving the renovation of the surrounding streets – needs to be completed to allow access.

“This phase of works is under the city’s supervision and is going slower,” said Think Tank Architecture. “We hope, and it’s in our client’s interest, that the market will be able to open by the end of this year.”

Other market architecture recently featured on Dezeen includes the multi-level Tepoztlán Market in central Mexico by local studios Ramírez Suarez Arquitectos and Laboratorio Regional de Arquitectura, and an open-air market in Colombia designed by Tarq Studio to accommodate community gatherings.

#9004. What's Love Got to Do With It? The Relationship Cycle Explained

Relationships aren’t just about candlelit dinners and cozy sofa nights — they’re complex AF, filled with ups, downs, twists, and turns. From the first flush of love to the settled comfort of commitment, relationships have stages that evolve with time.

Each relationship phase serves a unique purpose, helping you learn more about each other, yourself, and the kind of relationship you want to build. Understanding the dynamics of these stages is crucial for any couple (or throuple!) aiming to develop a lasting bond.

Whether you’re in the throes of a new romance or navigating the challenges of a long-term commitment, continue reading to learn how to rock each phase like a pro.

From those “can’t eat, can’t sleep” early days to the “let’s build an empire” moments, each relationship stage is like a season of your fave drama binge. But, like any good drama, the plot thickens as time passes and things change. Here’s what to expect, month by month:

Welcome to the love bubble, where everything about your significant other seems nothing short of magical. The positives overshadow any negatives, creating a blissfully skewed balance sheet of love. It lasts from about 6 months to 2 years for most peeps, but many folks say they are still madly in love even after 20 years together!

Research shows that during this stage, the prefrontal cortex, which is crucial for critically judging others, shows decreased activity. In other words, you’re less likely to focus on your partner’s faults and more likely to overlook their flaws.

Lurve also activates specific areas in the brain that are driven by goals and rewards. These areas are rich in dopamine and oxytocin receptors, chemicals that make you feel good and bonded to others. They encourage you to pursue and maintain a relationship because it feels rewarding and fulfilling.

If the euphoric stage is the wild, pulse-racing party of love, the early attachment stage is the cozy after-party where things get real comfortable. In the thrilling initial phase, your brain is doped up on dopamine, but as this initial buzz begins to mellow, a more sophisticated part of the brain starts to step up — the ventral pallidum.

Now, after the first year or so, deeper bonds are formed, helped along by attachment hormones like vasopressin and oxytocin, also fondly known as “the love hormone.” These hormones help transform the electric excitement of new love into a warm, enduring attachment.

Hold tight because the crisis stage hits around 5 to 7 years, and it’s a true test of your relationship’s resilience. This phase often feels like a rollercoaster, where life’s challenges can either pull you apart or push you closer together. Many couples experience a drift during this time, and how you handle it — either by addressing the issues head-on or continuing to drift — can define your future together.

Significant life events, like becoming parents, often occur during this stage and can intensify the pressure. These events can either strengthen your bond through shared responsibilities and mutual love or strain it to the breaking point. Successfully navigating this stage means moving beyond mere survival to fostering a deeper, more meaningful connection.

If you’ve made it this far, congrats, you’re in the deep attachment stage! Post-crisis, you’re looking at 7 years and beyond where you settle into that deep, comfy love. No more daily fireworks — now it’s about a slow-burning ember that warms the house.

You know each other inside and out, warts and all. It’s about unconditional support, knowing looks across crowded rooms, and being each other’s rock. Welcome to the good life!

Every relationship is a blend of sweet and sour and everything in between. Understanding the stages, from the initial euphoria to the deep attachment stage, helps you embrace the journey, keep your bond strong, and prepare your heart for whatever comes next. So buckle up and enjoy the ride — it’ll be worth it!

#9002. Vienna Museum’s Mummified Remains Reveal Cats Lived and Died Brutally in Ancient Egypt

Executive Editor, ARTnews & Art in America

Cats in ancient Egypt may have endured nine exceptionally hard lives, according to findings related to feline skulls in the collection of the Natural History Museum in Vienna.

As reported by Popular Mechanics, research on 131 skulls from a funerary site in Middle Egypt led by zooarchaeologist Wim Van Neer of the Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences revealed “disturbing” evidence that the cats may have been killed for the sake of offerings to the goddess known as Bastet. “Fourteen of the skulls show traumatic injuries, including blunt-force and sharp-force trauma,” the report reads. “Beyond fight wounds, some injuries were inflicted long enough before death to show signs of healing, which suggests that the animals may have endured physical violence from humans while still alive.” Related Articles Monumental Equestrian Statue of Roman Emperor Once Stood in Second Century Scotland Moab Petroglyphs Discovered Vandalized: 'Irreplaceable Cultural Resources'

It gets worse: “The cats’ treatment before death also seems to have been deplorable. Although no ancient records describe how the cats were kept, the researchers inferred that they were probably held in crowded enclosures. This could explain the fights, as well as the attacks on domestic cats by jungle cats, which were caught in marshlands or along the banks of the Nile when Egypt was lusher than it is today.”

The research, published in the Journal of Archaeological Science, also shared grim news regarding the manner in which the killed cats met their ends. “Skull fractures were the most common cause of death, whereas evidence of strangulation occurred less frequently,” the researchers said. “Our observations of traumatic lesions on the skulls provide evidence of fatal injuries, as well as cases of animals that survived violent interactions with humans.”

Architecture studios Formafantasma and Gonzalez Haase AAS have worked with Ferrari Style creative director Rocco Iannone on the brand’s first permanent store in New York, clad in a metallic facade.

Located in Manhattan’s SoHo neighbourhood, the flagship store for Ferrari’s fashion label is in a long, narrow building at the corner of Prince Street and Mercer Street and spreads across two levels.

Berlin-based Gonzalez Haase AAS clad the building in brushed metal, with curved window mullions covering floor-to-ceiling glass along its length.

It considers “the workshop as a junction at which artistic instinct, scientific rigour, craftsmanship and mechanical precision converge,” according to the team.

“The Officina is the place where intuition is given form through discipline, and where the human touch works in harmony with mechanical precision,” said Iannone.

The opening follows another Ferrari Style store opened earlier this year in London, designed by the same team, and both stores share pops of red, warm beige finishes, and steel accents.

However, the New York space was designed to fit in with the city. The team said the New York location reflects the “form, scale and material character of SoHo”.

“For New York, we wanted to translate this spirit into a space in which architecture, fashion and object design each retain their own identity while contributing to a single Ferrari language,” said the team.

“Every material and detail has been chosen to express this balance between art and science, creating an environment that is open, evolving and in direct dialogue with the energy of SoHo.”

Men’s ready-to-wear is located on the first floor, with objects displayed on units designed by Formafantasma.

#9000. Vibration Plate Benefits, According to a Weightlifting Coach

Vibration plates are like mini surfboards that give you a good shimmy while you’re exercising. Though you won’t find a mountain of extensive research behind them, you may be impressed by their possible benefits.

We asked a weightlifting coach to explain and show us how to add good vibrations to our workout routine.

These machines, which look like platforms or scales, are designed to activate something called whole-body vibration (WBV). WBV makes the body work harder by forcing it to contract muscles automatically.

Fans of WBV like to perform classic exercises on top of these machines, including:

Research points to WBV’s ability to boost blood flow.

Weightlifting coach Jarrod Nobbe explains that vibration plates help move blood by stimulating muscle contractions through rapid vibrations.

“The rhythmic contraction and relaxation of muscles help pump blood more efficiently throughout the body,” he says.

As Nobbe adds, movement generally increases blood flow and core temperature, preparing the body for activity. This means vibration plates may be an excellent warm-up activity.

A 2021 study showed that WBV can be an alternative exercise for older adults, boosting the effects of strengthening exercise.

Nobbe says this is because WBV engages muscles in a way that mimics resistance training.

“The vibrations activate and force muscles to contract and relax multiple times per second, which can lead to gains in muscle strength and endurance over time, especially when combined with specific exercises,” he says.

Nobbe points to some anecdotal evidence suggesting that regular use of vibration plates may help boost energy levels, possibly thanks to increased blood circulation and enhanced muscle activation.

“Ultimately, I stand by the idea that movement is medicine,” Nobbe says. “Tons of research already proves that regular physical activity boosts mood, mental health, and promotes energy levels.”

Nobbe says WBV may reduce muscle soreness, stiffness, and inflammation by encouraging blood flow to the muscles. This, he explains, aids in faster recovery post-exercise or injury.

WBV has been shown to improve bone mineral density, which Nobbe points out may positively affect those at risk of osteoporosis.

“The mechanical vibrations stimulate bone cells, potentially leading to increased bone density and strength, delivering the same positive bone health benefits of resistance training,” he says.

“Unfortunately, vibration plates aren’t a one-stop shop for weight loss,” Nobbe says.

He explains that vibration plates alone are unlikely to significantly reduce belly fat without dietary changes and additional exercise.

“While vibration plates can contribute to overall calorie expenditure and muscle activation, targeted fat loss requires a comprehensive approach including diet, cardio exercise, and resistance training,” he says.

These tips will help you stand on your vibration plate with a slight bend at your knee or perform exercises on top of it.

More research is needed around WBV — AKA what happens when you use a vibration plate — but existing smaller research is promising.

Use your machine carefully, and remember to maintain a healthy lifestyle and workout routine.

#8998. Ocean liner sunk in Florida to become "world's largest artificial reef"

Photography courtesy of Destin-Fort Walton Beach

On Wednesday, the ocean liner SS United States was sunk 180 feet underwater to become an artificial reef off the coast of Florida.

The sinking took approximately eight hours, and dozens of onlookers and officials looked on as the ship underwent a controlled deployment, or scuttling, to the bottom of the ocean.

The ship will join a long stretch of artificial reefs, including 580 other decommissioned vessels and structures, that line the ocean floor off the coast Destin-Fort Walton Beach, Florida.

“A new chapter has begun in Destin-Fort Walton Beach, Florida, where the legendary SS United States, once the fastest ocean liner in the world, has completed her final voyage to become the World’s Largest Artificial Reef,” said a release from the government of Destin-Fort Walton Beach.

The site serves as a tourist and dive destination for SCUBA divers both new and seasoned, as the underwater structures are meant to provide infrastructure for marine life.

“Beyond its appeal as a dive destination, the SS United States will serve an important environmental purpose,” said the team.

“Her massive structure will provide new habitat for marine life, supporting the growth of an underwater ecosystem that includes inhabitants such as sea turtles, grouper, snapper and marlin.”

In preparation for its scuttling, the ship underwent a years-long remediation process, where it was stripped of toxic materials, such as green neotex exterior floor covering and paint.

Elements such as the ventilation system, wiring and the propeller were also removed, with the latter stored for a land-based museum that will accompany the dive site.

“To see a project of this magnitude become a reality is an incredible moment for our team and for the future of marine conservation,” said Destin-Fort Walton Beach natural resources chief Alex Fogg.

“This is so much more than creating a new dive destination. It’s an opportunity to advance marine science on a scale we’ve never experienced before. The sheer scale of the SS United States presents a rare opportunity to study how an artificial reef of this size transforms over time.”

The project has been years in the making. The ship, designed by naval architect William Francis Gibb and known for its speed, served as a passenger vessel between 1952 and 1969.

It was decommissioned in 1969, and eventually bought to a Philadelphia harbour in the 1990s, where it sat inactive for decades as various owners bought and then sold the vessel in failed attempts to restore it and make it profitable.

In 2009, the non-profit SS United States Conservancy purchased and began stewarding the ship.

In 2024, due to rent issues, the ship could no longer stay berthed at its Philadelphia pier, and the SS United States Conservancy sold it to Okaloosa County, Florida, for $1 million.

As of today, it stands upright in its intended position, and its uppermost deck is accessible to divers, who can “now enjoy the site”.

Other artificial reefs around the world include the Reefline project in Miami, which is set to feature underwater sculpture designed by OMA and a LEGO-inspired modular system designed by Alex Goad, intended to restore damaged coral reefs.
