#8978. it’s a bird, it’s a plane, it’s funny weather! by theo triantafyllidis

as extreme weather becomes harder to predict, this installation imagines a future in which the weather itself becomes the narrator of our lives.

annalise kamegawa November 15, 2026 7 min

In Theo Triantafyllidis’s video-based installation, Funny Weather, software-generated birds, planes, and clouds drift across a dreamy sky. At any point, the weather can turn gray, a flock can burst across the screen, or a kite can whip into view. To create this work, the artist draws on real-time data local to Manchester, where the installation is presented, to generate an uncanny AI-powered simulation of the world outside the exhibition space. Funny Weather, which premieres in mid-November at Aviva Studios in the UK, will travel to Hong Kong, Melbourne, and New York. In each new city, the work will draw on local data, creating a site-specific reflection of the weather in that location.

In conversation with designboom, Triantafyllidis revealed the APIs he worked with, the parallels between weather forecasting and divination, and how weather is becoming ‘the main character’. On first receiving the commission, which will travel between four international hosts, he notes, ‘I had this idea of a weather oracle or this strange weather prediction machine as a start.’

above and banner by Theo Triantafyllidis, preview still for Funny Weather, 2026 | image courtesy the ArtistTheo Triantafyllidis’s Funny Weather at Aviva Studios | image by Michael Pollard, courtesy of Factory International

To create Funny Weather, Triantafyllidis drew on three data sets. The first was the Open-Meteo API, which provides weather information: blue skies, overcast conditions, and impending thunderstorms. The next was a flight radar that reported which flights were passing over Aviva Studios. The last, which Triantafyllidis admits was the ‘most interesting’ to work with, was eBird and Merlin Bird ID – tools that track and identify bird sightings. The sightings are self-reported by users, making them a very subjective data set to work with. He notes that the data collected in eBird is ‘a way of digitizing nature that is very personal and strange. It has a bit of competitiveness to it and a bit of true love for what people are looking at.’

‘These are getting pulled daily and within intervals and fed into our custom system,’ says Triantafyllidis of how this data is translated into the visuals seen on screen. ‘With each of these three data streams, we’re [feeding] into different components of the system and driving different things.’

Although he admits that these data sets feel disparate, the artist says he is creating a kind of uncanny universe. He explains, ‘what I’m trying to do is give this data to a custom language model that we’re running and ask it to [prophesize] based on this data.’ Inside Funny Weather is what Factory International describes as a ‘bespoke locally hosted AI Oracle’ that generates the environment within the simulation. Although powered by the latest technology, the process reflects a kind of ancient logic. Triantafyllidis says it is ‘like looking back at how forecasting and divination worked in earlier human history, when maybe people were more in tune with weather and natural patterns and the general flow of things.’ He calls the task he gives the program a ‘nonsensical premise’ when considering the seemingly arbitrary selection of bird, weather, and flight-path data points. But by merging this information and transforming it into a visual landscape, he hopes that it will ‘tell us something useful and meaningful about our future.’

When talking about the installation at Aviva Studios, the artist notes that ‘sometimes the weather of our system aligns with what we see outside.’ He describes the lobby where the massive screen sits, continually morphing in response to Funny Weather and the data fed into it. ‘You can’t see the sky exactly,’ he says of the Manchester space, ‘but you can get the sense of what’s the weather outside. And here is a system [Funny Weather] attempting to align itself with the weather outside – sometimes successfully, sometimes not so successfully.’ The data itself is sometimes a bit wonky or inaccurate, causing what Triantafyllidis calls ‘stress’ in the environment. He says that sometimes there will be an influx of planes or ‘there [will be] birds that are not supposed to be there either – too early for the season or very unique, rare birds that are not seen in the area very frequently. This will affect the mood of the system.’

‘I think climate change is such a hyper object that is very tough for the human mind to comprehend,’ says Triantafyllidis on the urgency of the themes in his work. ‘We’ve reached a tipping point with the instability of the weather where we’re starting to experience really crazy shifts and weird meteorological phenomena happening on a very day-to-day basis and in every part of the world.’ He goes on to talk about the increased frequency of these extreme climate patterns and how, inevitably, the weather will become ‘this main character in our lives.’ Funny Weather acknowledges this inevitability: ‘I’m trying to imagine a good way to let the weather be the narrator of these stories, giving it this strange voice that can communicate somehow through this weird system.’

#8977. Mecanoo transforms former gold vault into "city’s living room" in renovation of De Nederlandsche Bank in Amsterdam

Photography is by Ossip van Duivenbode courtesy of De Nederlandsche Bank

Dutch firm Mecanoo has completed a major renovation of the Netherlands’ central bank, which involved dismantling a 14-storey tower and opening up the former gold vault.

The Francine Houben-led architecture studio oversaw a complete retrofit of De Nederlandsche Bank, a 1968 structure that some had described as the nation’s ugliest building.

Located in the heart of Amsterdam, this huge concrete-slab building is in complete contrast to the city’s historic canal houses.

The original architect, Marius Frans Duintjer, had hoped to emulate the modernist works of Mies van der Rohe, but security requirements had resulted in “a fortress with fences, large boulders and armed military police,” according to Mecanoo.

The building was further complicated by later extensions, which included an extra storey above the low-rise main building and a cylindrical 14-storey tower built alongside the original central tower.

Mecanoo’s transformation was enabled by the relocation of gold reserves and banknote operations to a location in Zeist.

This allowed the architects to give the building a sense of transparency and openness that was envisioned from the outset, but had never been possible before now.

The project is an exemplar for sustainable renovation, as proven by its nomination for Dezeen Awards 2026.

Removing the cylindrical tower was pivotal, as it allowed space for a new public garden at the heart of the scheme.

This tower was carefully dismantled, allowing many materials to be reused.

Salvaged concrete was used to build a new quay beside the canal, while the rest was donated to social housing projects in the city.

The removal enabled a reorganisation of the ground floor.

The entrance was relocated to Frederiksplein, while floorplates were cut away to reveal the 61-metre-long former vault, which has been transformed into an exhibition gallery.

“The most secretive part of the bank is now its most public,” said Mecanoo.

“Inside the vault, visitors can immerse themselves in exhibitions and interactive games that tell the story of gold, money, the economy and DNB’s core activities.”

The retained structures were newly clad in red ceramic bricks. These incorporate the brown tiles that clad the building previously, with the old tiles crushed for use as pigment.

These combine with new glazing, a Kastenfenster system of ventilated double-glazing with integrated sun shading, which has helped to reduce the building’s day-to-day energy requirements by an estimated 80 per cent.

Inside, the space linking the vault with the courtyard was designed as an indoor street, with seating areas along the edges and auditoriums (one formal, the other informal) at each end.

“Francine Houben’s inspiration came from the vibrant ‘street’ of the central hall in the former Faculty of Architecture building at TU Delft, which was destroyed by fire,” said Mecanoo.

The rest of the building is organised into zones with varying levels of security.

A five-storey atrium organises the semi-public area, which includes a meeting centre and a restaurant overlooking the Singelgracht, while the more secure employee zones are located in both the courtyard building and the tower.

The meeting centre occupies what was previously a double-height cash hall, with distinctive tree-like columns.

The original spiral staircase still stands, alongside a second added by Mecanoo, while custom-designed tables feature integrated lamps.

Timber was used for many of the new surfaces, including a slatted ceiling made from locally felled poplar trees.

Shades of red, blue and orange extend across other surfaces and interior elements, including walls covered in recycled-plastic felt, carpets and furniture.

“The colour scheme is inspired by the vibrant paper currency from the last period of the Dutch guilder,” said Mecanoo.

The interiors are completed by DNB’s collection of artwork, energy-efficient lighting systems and circular planting boxes.

“The renovation transforms De Nederlandsche Bank from a closed fortress into a transparent circular landmark, repurposing the former gold vault as the city’s living room for the public,” concluded Mecanoo.

Other recent projects by the firm include the rock-like Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi, the tile-clad Villa BW and the book-inspired Macau Central Library.

#8975. Skin in the Game: Is Adapalene or Salicylic Acid Better for Acne?

If you have acne, you probably know more about skincare than most people. You might even impress friends with terms like “adapalene” and “salicylic acid.”

But do you know what each treatment does for your skin and if one is better for acne? Let’s find out!

Salicylic acid is a keratolytic agent commonly found in over-the-counter creams, face washes, masks, and gels. While it’s often used for acne, it can also help with dandruff, psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis, calluses, and warts.

Adapalene, often known by its brand name Differin, is a topical retinoid. It comes in various forms, such as gels, cleansers, and creams. And just like salicylic acid, it’s available over-the-counter without a prescription.

On a chemical level, adapalene and salicylic acid work in different ways to clear acne.

Salicylic acid breaks down a protein called keratin in the outer layer of the skin. Studies show this helps remove the buildup of dead skin cells. It also reduces inflammation in the skin, calming the redness that often comes with breakouts.

Adapalene, on the other hand, is a retinoid. And what, you may ask, is a retinoid? It’s a derivative of vitamin A that attaches to receptors in the skin. Doing so prompts cell turnover to speed up, helping skin regenerate more quickly and lowering the likelihood of clogged pores.

So… what do these differences mean for acne? Both adapalene and salicylic acid can treat skin prone to breakouts (though it’s not recommended to use them together since this can over-irritate your skin).

Which one is more potent may depend on your acne type. Research shows that adapalene was among the best treatments for comedonal acne (aka whiteheads and blackheads), whereas salicylic acid was less effective and more affordable.

Long story short: Your dermatologist can help determine which is the smarter choice for your type of acne.

Studies haven’t directly compared adapalene and salicylic acid for blackheads, but both can help. Blackheads form from plugged hair follicles, and salicylic acid’s exfoliating action can clear clogged pores. Adapalene increases cell turnover, which can also help remove blackheads.

Adapalene is a retinoid. Retinoids are well-established anti-aging agents because they stimulate new cell growth and promote collagen production. Some studies have also shown anti-aging benefits from salicylic acid.

While salicylic acid, due to its exfoliating properties, can help reduce wrinkles, adapalene is generally more effective for addressing aging-related concerns like wrinkles.

Adapalene is an over-the-counter acne treatment — so prescription-strength options may work better. According to the American Academy of Dermatology, some of the most potent acne treatments include antibiotics and isotretinoin.

Adapalene isn’t a magic wand for acne. It may be an ideal choice for some people, but depending on your skin type and sensitivity level, salicylic acid, other OTC products, or even a prescription treatment might be your best bet.

Research shows that adapalene can be just as strong for zapping zits as benzoyl peroxide (another potentially powerful weapon in the battle against acne). A 2024 study, for example, found that 0.1% topical adapalene was as safe and effective as a 4% benzoyl peroxide solution in people of color.

Though adapalene may be an effective acne treatment, it’s not the pinnacle of retinoid strength. Of the four “generations” of retinoids, adapalene is considered third-generation. Fourth-generation retinoids are typically stronger and have higher specificity to retinoic acid receptors in the skin. For this reason, they’re available only by prescription.

Feel free to experiment with adapalene and salicylic acid to see which works best for you — after all, it’s your face! You might find one more effective for your skin. For expert advice, be sure to consult your dermatologist.

Last medically reviewed on July 31, 2024

#8974. Reims 502 uses pink palette for "non-referential" commercial building in Mexico

A stepped facade fronts this pink commercial building in Mexico called Rosadoce, designed by local studio Reims 502 to suit various tenants over its lifespan.

Rosadoce is located in a low-density residential neighbourhood near the historic centre of Querétaro, a state in north-central Mexico, which is redeveloping into a mixed-use area.

The studio said the 840-square-metre building was “conceived as an adaptable urban asset” that can function as a single unit, four independent commercial spaces or sixteen smaller modules, ensuring its longevity and usability well into the future.

“Rosadoce by Reims 502 is a flexible commercial building in Querétaro, Mexico, designed as an adaptable urban platform for work, commerce and public life,” said the studio.

“Designed during the pandemic, it rethinks commercial architecture in response to changing patterns of work, consumption and urban life.”

Local planning constraints determined the building’s scale, while its “non-referential form” evolved from various design strategies, the studio said.

It reaches seven metres in height – the maximum height allowed above street level – which led the studio to carve out a semi-basement level to increase usable area.

Above ground are two open-plan levels, organised around a central stair and punctured by vertical voids that naturally light and ventilate the building.

Meanwhile, the basement currently contains service spaces including parking and plant rooms. However, similarly to the rest of the building, it has an open-plan layout to support future commercial activity.

Crowning Rosadoce is a usable rooftop filled with planters that provide thermal insulation.

“The inverted-stair facade creates horizontal openings for daylight and views while regulating visual permeability from the street,” said the studio.

“Because the building’s future uses remain open-ended, the facade avoids excessive transparency and provides a controlled threshold between public exposure and interior flexibility.”

The pink render that colours the building’s exterior, provided by lime-based products manufacturer Nanocal, was chosen as a nod to the rose-colored quarry stone that defines Querétaro’s historic centre.

This same colour was used throughout the project, with the steel structure, concrete blockwork, grilles and service equipment all finished in the same tone, creating a warm feel for the interior.

According to the studio, the building’s future flexibility is achieved through the combination of open plans as well as “exposed construction, passive environmental strategies and an active rooftop”.

“This allows it to respond to different economic scenarios, tenant profiles, subletting arrangements and future programmes without major structural alterations,” said Reims 502.

The project is on the eight-strong shortlist for the small workplace interior category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards.

Other pink buildings in Mexico include a co-living apartment block with a series of arched forms by Estudio Zero and a minimalist house sandwiched between two buildings by César Béjar Studio.

#8973. SP architects gives antalya’s former expo grounds a second life for COP31

an 88-hectare campus reuses existing pavilions and introduces shaded walkways, modular structures and public spaces intended to outlast the climate summit.

Antalya’s former EXPO 2016 site has taken on a second assignment. As COP31 runs in the Turkish city from November 9 to 20, SP Architects has transformed the 875,117-square-meter horticultural exhibition grounds in Aksu into a conference campus for diplomats, scientists, civil society and visitors. Rather than begin with a blank site, the firm has worked with the existing landscape of gardens, a lake, an observation tower and exhibition halls, folding the infrastructure of one international gathering into another.

Around 65,000 square meters of existing buildings have been brought back into use, while additional spaces combine permanent construction with modular systems intended for later reuse. SP Architects led the project from concept through construction, operating from an office established on site and coordinating with Turkey’s Ministry of Environment, Urbanisation and Climate Change and the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). It is a rather practical answer to a familiar question: how much new building should a climate conference really require?

The 393,461-square-meter Blue Zone houses the official UNFCCC negotiations and facilities for accredited participants. Its 170,394 square meters of usable space include two general assembly halls seating 1,600 and 815 delegates, 28 meeting rooms, 15 bilateral meeting rooms, and extensive media facilities. At the entrance, a 5,400-square-meter registration building is sheltered by a perforated canopy, whose patterned screens filter the strong Mediterranean sunlight. A covered promenade, lined with slender arches, a lightweight textile canopy, timber decks and a reflecting water channel, connects the different spaces.

Across the site, the 481,656-square-meter Green Zone is dedicated to exhibitions and public engagement. Nearly half of its 94,435 square meters of usable area occupies existing Expo structures, including the convention center, indoor gardens, the Children’s Science and Technology Museum, and open-air amphitheaters. New thematic blocks explore subjects ranging from energy transition and cultural heritage to technology, innovation and climate finance. Exhibition pavilions are complemented by meeting rooms, lounges, podcast studios and informal gathering areas, allowing conversations to unfold beyond the official negotiating tables.

Throughout the complex, SP Architects has sought to balance the demanding requirements of an international diplomatic event with a more adaptable architectural framework. New permanent and temporary structures are integrated into the existing grounds, with modular and reusable components intended to limit unnecessary construction. The approach places particular emphasis on environmental control, operational efficiency and flexible circulation, while making the most of the site’s landscaped setting. Beyond the architectural gestures, the reuse of existing buildings forms a central part of the project’s environmental strategy.

Once COP31 concludes on November 20, the plan is for the grounds to remain active as a venue for fairs, concerts and other events, in coordination with Antalya’s metropolitan and district municipalities. For SP Architects, the redevelopment represents an investment in the city’s future rather than a temporary backdrop for international diplomacy. Whether that promised second life materializes will be an important measure of the project’s sustainability, long after the delegates, cameras and climate declarations have moved on.

architects: SP Architects | @sparchitects.global

Sign up at biltrewards.com. No annual fee, no hard pull for the initial application check. Once approved, download the Bilt app and register your rent payment address.

Add five small recurring charges to your Bilt card (streaming services, subscriptions, or small autopay bills). This ensures you hit the monthly minimum to earn points on rent without thinking about it.

If your building is in the Bilt Alliance, payments are seamless. If not, Bilt processes the payment via ACH to your landlord. Confirm the first payment clears successfully.

Link your World of Hyatt account in the Bilt app. Transfer points at a 1:1 ratio. Transfers are instant, so only move points when you have a specific redemption in mind.

Search Hyatt.com for award availability at your target property. Start with a Category 3-4 property for your first redemption to see the system work end-to-end before targeting aspirational stays.

Imagine checking into a Park Hyatt — marble floors, a sommelier who remembers your name by day two, a room that costs $400 a night — and knowing you paid for it with points you earned by writing your rent check. Not by flying 100,000 miles. Not by spending on a business credit card. By paying the bill you were already going to pay anyway. That's the emotional core of this sweet spot, and it's one of the most powerful entry points into travel rewards for the ChooseFI community. Rent is typically your single largest monthly expense, and for years it was a dead end — money out the door with zero return. Bilt Rewards changed that equation entirely. Here's the math that should stop you mid-scroll: a single night at a Category 4 Hyatt — think Hyatt Place in a major city or a solid Park Hyatt property in a secondary market — costs around $150–$250 in cash. With World of Hyatt points, that same night runs 15,000 points. Transfer your Bilt points at a 1:1 ratio, and you've just redeemed at roughly 1–1.7 cents per point at the low end. But at a Category 6 or 7 property — a Grand Hyatt in Tokyo, a Alila in Bali, an Andaz on the Sunset Strip — cash rates climb to $350–$600 per night while the award chart holds steady. That's where you hit **4–8 cents per point**, the upper end of what any hotel currency in the world delivers. The CPP range for this redemption runs **2–8 cents per point**, with a retail value of **$100–$400 per redemption unit**. In loyalty currency terms, that's elite-tier performance. Most hotel points deliver 0.5–0.8 cents. Hyatt points, earned through your rent payment and transferred instantly, routinely deliver 3–5x that value. This is a **pricing inefficiency built into Hyatt's fixed award chart**. Hyatt hasn't aggressively devalued the way other programs have. The chart still prices aspirational properties at points levels that don't reflect their true cash cost — and Bilt gives you a direct pipeline to those points through the expense you can't avoid. For anyone on the path to FI, that's not a hack. That's just math working in your favor.

Why rent-to-hotel is one of the most accessible travel rewards sweet spots

The core insight here has two parts, and understanding both will change how you think about every dollar of rent you pay going forward.

Part One: Bilt Is the Only Card That Earns Points on Rent With No Fee

Most landlords don't accept credit cards. Those that do typically charge a 2–3% processing fee, which instantly erases any rewards value. Bilt solved this by partnering directly with property management companies and creating a system where you pay rent via the Bilt app, and the payment processes as ACH (no fee to you or your landlord), while Bilt credits your account with points. You earn 1x point per dollar on rent, up to 100,000 points per year. On a $2,000/month rent payment, that's 24,000 Hyatt points annually from a bill you were paying anyway. Zero incremental spend. Zero fees.

The one rule to know: you must make at least 5 transactions on your Bilt card each statement period to earn points on rent. Five purchases — even five $1 transactions — unlocks the rent earnings. This is a simple, low-lift requirement.

Part Two: World of Hyatt's Fixed Award Chart Is the Unlock

Once your Bilt points are sitting in your account, you transfer them to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio, and the transfer is instant. No waiting 3–5 business days. No points in limbo while availability disappears. You search, you find availability, you transfer, you book — in a single session if you want.

Hyatt's award chart is category-based, fixed pricing from 3,500 points (Category 1) to 45,000 points (Category 8) per night. This is the inefficiency. When a Park Hyatt in a major international city costs $500 in cash but only 30,000 points (Category 6), you're extracting 1.67 cents per point at minimum — and in peak season when cash rates hit $700, you're at 2.3+ cpp. The chart doesn't move with cash prices.

What makes this particularly powerful for the ChooseFI community is the no fuel surcharges policy — Hyatt charges zero fuel surcharges on award stays, so 15,000 points always means exactly 15,000 points out of your account. No surprise $75 "carrier fees" tacked on at checkout.

The transfer path is: Bilt Rewards → World of Hyatt at 1:1, instant. Chase Ultimate Rewards also transfers to Hyatt at 1:1 instantly, which means if you hold a Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve, you have a second pipeline to the same program — an important redundancy for maximizing this sweet spot.

For 5,000 points — a single night at a Category 1 or 2 property — you're looking at a $100–$150 night that might cost you 2.5 months of coffee purchases on the Bilt card. That's the entry point. The ceiling is a $400+ night at a Category 5–7 property for 20,000–30,000 points. Both ends of the spectrum represent exceptional value, which is rare in any loyalty program.

Head to biltrewards.com and apply for the Bilt Mastercard (issued by Wells Fargo). The card has no annual fee. Once approved, add the card to your Bilt app and register your rent payment. If your building is in the Bilt Alliance (a growing network of partnered properties), setup is seamless. If not, you can still pay rent through the Bilt app via ACH transfer — Bilt mails a check to your landlord on your behalf, and you still earn points.

Key setup rule: Activate rent rewards in the app before your first payment cycle.

Before rent points post, you need five qualifying purchases on your Bilt card that statement period. Set up small recurring charges — a streaming subscription, a coffee shop, a weekly grocery run — and you'll hit this automatically. Don't forget this step; missing it means forfeiting that month's rent points.

Go to world.hyatt.com and use the award availability search. Select "Use Points" and search your destination and dates. Hyatt's search shows availability up to 395 days in advance — one of the longest windows in the hotel loyalty space. Identify your property, confirm the points price and availability, then — and only then — proceed to transfer.

Never transfer points without confirmed availability. Even though Hyatt availability is generally strong, you want to lock in what you see before moving irreversible points.

In the Bilt app, navigate to "Redeem" → "Transfer Points" and select World of Hyatt. Enter the exact number of points you need. The transfer is instant — points appear in your Hyatt account within minutes, not days. This is one of Bilt's most underrated features and means you can act on last-minute availability without risk.

Return to world.hyatt.com, confirm your points balance has updated, and complete your booking. You'll pay zero fuel surcharges — the points cost is the only cost. You can also call the World of Hyatt reservations line if you need help with a complex booking or want to stack a free night certificate.

If your first-choice property is sold out on points, try these tactics:

Hotel loyalty programs use "award charts" that assign each property a category level with a fixed points price. When a hotel's cash rate rises due to demand or location, the points price stays the same. This creates the value gap that makes points redemptions worthwhile. Hyatt's chart is considered the most generous among major hotel chains because it has resisted the aggressive devaluations that Hilton and Marriott have implemented. A Category 7 property might cost $500-$800 per night in cash but only 30,000 points. That gap is where your 4-8 cents per point value comes from.

Let's make this concrete. You've been paying $1,800/month in rent for the past year, diligently hitting your five monthly transactions. Your Bilt account holds approximately 21,600 points (1x on rent, plus some bonus earning on the card). You're planning a long weekend in Nashville with your partner.

The Property: Hyatt Place Nashville Downtown. Category 3, costing 12,000 World of Hyatt points per night. Cash rate for a Friday–Sunday stay: $189/night, totaling $378 for two nights before taxes and fees. With taxes, you're looking at roughly $430 out of pocket.

The Points Play: Transfer 24,000 Bilt points to Hyatt instantly, book two nights. Total points spent: 24,000. Total cash paid: $0 (Hyatt charges no fuel surcharges, no award fees).

The CPP calculation: $378 cash value ÷ 24,000 points = 1.58 cents per point at the conservative end. Factor in the taxes you're also avoiding (most properties don't charge taxes on award stays), and your effective CPP climbs closer to 1.8–2 cents per point.

Now scale up. Apply the same 24,000 points to a single night at Park Hyatt Chicago — a Category 7 property. Cash rate: $550–$700/night on a peak weekend. Points cost: 30,000 per night (you'll need to save a couple extra months). At $600 cash value for 30,000 points, you're at 2 cents per point — but if you hit a $700 night, that's 2.33 cpp.

The experience itself? Park Hyatt properties deliver: floor-to-ceiling windows, complimentary minibar items, a spa, and a level of service that genuinely doesn't feel like a "points hotel." You're not using a coupon at a budget chain — you're staying at the same property business travelers expense at full rate, experiencing everything they experience, funded almost entirely by the rent check you wrote anyway.

If you hold Hyatt Globalist status, suite upgrades on award stays are available based on availability — turning a 30,000-point redemption into a $900+ suite night. That's where the CPP ceiling of 8 cents per point becomes real.

World of Hyatt awards include a fifth-night-free benefit on standard award redemptions when you book five or more consecutive nights. On a five-night stay at a Category 5 property (20,000 points/night), you'd normally pay 100,000 points — but with the fifth night free, it's 80,000 points for five nights. That's a 20% improvement in value with zero extra effort. Plan longer trips to unlock this.

Do: Book 395 Days Out for Peak Destinations

Hyatt opens award inventory at the same time as cash inventory — 395 days in advance. For high-demand properties (think Park Hyatt Maldives at Hadahaa or Alila Ventana Big Sur), availability at standard rates disappears quickly. Set a calendar reminder and search early.

If you hold a Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve, your Chase Ultimate Rewards points also transfer to Hyatt at 1:1, instantly. This means you have two separate point pools feeding the same program — Bilt for rent earnings and Chase for everyday spending. Together, you can accumulate Hyatt points significantly faster and take on higher-category properties.

Avoid: Transferring Points Before Confirming Availability

Bilt-to-Hyatt transfers are instant and irreversible. If you transfer 30,000 points and then can't find the availability you thought you saw, those points are now in Hyatt — and if you don't use them, they expire after 24 months of account inactivity. Always search Hyatt first, confirm dates and property, then transfer.

Avoid: Missing the 5-Transaction Monthly Minimum

This is the most common Bilt mistake. If you forget to make five purchases on your Bilt card in a given month, you earn zero points on rent — not reduced points, zero. Automate five small recurring charges to the card and never think about it again.

Do: Target Category 4–6 Properties for Best Value

Category 1–3 properties offer solid value, but the CPP accelerates meaningfully in Categories 4–6 (15,000–25,000 points/night) where cash rates are $200–$400 but points costs haven't kept pace. This is the sweet spot within the sweet spot.

Do: Watch for Hyatt's Points + Cash Awards

Hyatt offers a Points + Cash option at roughly half the standard award rate, combined with a cash co-pay. If your Hyatt balance is small, this lets you access properties without waiting to accumulate a full award.

This redemption was built for renters — specifically, renters who are already on the path to FI and feel the friction of paying rent every month with nothing to show for it. If you pay at least $1,000/month in rent, this sweet spot is generating meaningful Hyatt points from dollar one. At $2,000/month, you're accumulating 24,000 Hyatt points per year from rent alone — enough for two nights at a Category 5 property or a single aspirational night at a Park Hyatt.

Minimum to make it work: You need at least 5,000 Hyatt points for a Category 1 redemption — easily achievable after 5–6 months of rent payments on a $1,000/month lease. For aspirational Category 6–7 stays, you're targeting 25,000–30,000 points, which takes planning but is absolutely achievable.

This isn't the right fit if you own your home (no rent to earn on), if you're already deep into a competing hotel loyalty program, or if your primary travel goal is international business class flights — in that case, transferable airline currencies deserve more of your attention first. But for hotel stays, especially in the U.S., this is the single most frictionless on-ramp into the Hyatt ecosystem available anywhere.

This redemption earns a **5/5 for beginner friendliness**, and that rating is accurate — but it helps to understand exactly *why* it's easy, so you don't accidentally make it harder than it needs to be. **What makes it easy:** - Earning is passive. Once your Bilt card is set up and rent is registered, points accrue automatically with no behavior change required (beyond five small monthly transactions). - The transfer is instant — no waiting, no uncertainty, no risk of availability disappearing while points are in transit. - Hyatt's award chart is fixed and transparent. You can see exactly what a property costs before you transfer a single point. - No fuel surcharges means no unpleasant surprises at checkout. **The one area that trips beginners up:** forgetting the five-transaction monthly minimum. This is the single most common Bilt mistake, and it's entirely preventable. Set up five small autopay charges on your Bilt card — a $5 streaming service, a recurring Amazon purchase, anything — and you'll never miss it. **Tip for the first redemption:** Start with a Category 3 or 4 Hyatt Place or Hyatt Regency for a domestic weekend trip. The points requirement is low (8,000–15,000 points), availability is widely open, and the booking process is identical to any other Hyatt stay. It's a low-stakes way to see the entire system work from earning to booking. If you can pay rent, own a smartphone, and make five purchases a month, you can execute this redemption. The ChooseFI community has embraced this one for good reason — it's genuinely the most accessible entry point into premium hotel travel rewards available today.

No. Bilt works with any landlord that accepts payment. If your building is not in the Bilt Alliance, Bilt processes the payment via ACH. The only difference is Alliance buildings may offer additional perks like bonus points or rent credits.

You will still pay your rent through Bilt, but you will earn zero points on that month's rent payment. The five-transaction requirement resets monthly. Set up autopay on small recurring charges to prevent this.

Yes. Bilt transfers to over a dozen airline and hotel partners including American Airlines, United, Air Canada Aeroplan, and IHG. However, Hyatt consistently delivers the highest cents-per-point value among hotel transfer partners.

Bilt caps rent earning at 100,000 points per month (equivalent to $100,000 in rent at 1x). For the vast majority of renters, this cap is irrelevant. There is no annual cap on total points earned.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

The Bilt-to-Hyatt pipeline is the most accessible travel rewards sweet spot available today. You are already paying rent. The Bilt card has no annual fee. Hyatt points deliver 2-8 cents in value. The transfer is instant. If you rent and you are not earning Hyatt points from that rent payment, you are leaving hundreds of dollars in annual hotel value on the table. Start with one Category 3-4 weekend stay to see it work, then scale up to aspirational properties as your balance grows.

#8971. Thai Massage Therapy: Benefits and What to Expect

Feeling stressed? Whether you unwind with yoga or a relaxing massage, Thai massage combines the best of both worlds, benefiting your mind and body. Here’s everything you need to know!

Thai massage is a special kind of bodywork that blends relaxation with flexibility. Think of it as a gentle, full-body, more active experience. It’s all about boosting your flexibility and energizing your body. Just a heads-up: napping during a Thai massage might be a challenge!

Drawing from Ayurvedic and traditional Chinese medicine, this ancient technique mixes assisted yoga stretches, acupressure, and soothing rocking for 60 to 90 minutes. Unlike Western-style massages at a local spa, Thai massage takes place on a mat on the floor. A certified therapist will work to stretch your muscles and apply pressure along your body’s energy lines, known as sen, to release stress with a graceful, rhythmic touch.

You can schedule a Thai massage at many spas, massage clinics, and even some yoga studios, but make sure you find someone with the proper training and certification to give you an authentic experience.

When you arrive for a Thai massage, you might be given some comfy clothes, like a T-shirt and drawstring pants. You’ll remove your shoes, silence your phone, place your jewelry in a small dish, and settle onto a floor mat. Before the session, let the therapist know if you have any injuries.

If this is your first session, it can be intense, so focus on breathing and relaxing. You’ll likely start on your back, with the therapist beginning on your feet and legs. Since the therapist uses their body weight to guide you, it might initially feel a bit weird. Some discomfort is normal as your body stretches, but don’t hesitate to let your therapist know if anything feels uncomfortable.As the session progresses, you’ll likely switch positions, including flipping onto your belly or trying various other postures. Go with the flow as your therapist guides you through stretches and yoga-like moves designed to open up your joints, move your energy, and release tension. Keep breathing and communicate with your therapist throughout the process.

As the session wraps up, you’ll enjoy some gentle rocking motions to ease you out of the massage. You might feel sore afterward, especially if it’s your first Thai massage, so hydrate and rest. You’ll likely feel incredibly relaxed, more flexible, and energized.

Pro tip: Clear your mind and be open to guidance. While the stretches may feel awkward initially, allow yourself to let go. This can help you fully experience the massage’s benefits.

Your Thai massage experience won’t resemble a Western-style deep tissue massage. You won’t be naked under a sheet on a raised massage table, and the massage therapist won’t be using long, deep strokes to work your muscles.The other significant difference is that, like some forms of yoga, Thai massage has a spiritual element based on Buddhism. As they use the weight of their bodies to work on your body, your therapist is also trained to send you kind, loving, healing vibes. The ultimate goal is to help you feel better by allowing your energy to flow throughout your body.

The ancient practice of Thai massage combines assisted yoga stretches, acupressure, and rhythmic rocking to unknot your body and get your inner energy flowing. Unlike Western massage techniques, you’ll be fully clothed on a floor mat, with the massage therapist using their entire body to release your tension.

Permit yourself to let go, and expect an active, sometimes intense, full-body experience that leaves you relaxed and energized.

Last medically reviewed on July 31, 2024

#8970. Tant A Temps Design "restores the visual characteristics of Tang architecture" in Chinese cafe

Local practice Tant A Temps Design aimed to revive the aesthetics of the Tang Dynasty when designing the interiors for cafe Laibei 1087, located in a historical building in Xi’an, China.

The cafe sits inside the Beilin Museum, originally constructed in 1087 to preserve stone steles inscribed with Confucian philosophy and famous calligraphic works.

The timber columns and beams of the historic building were preserved, with the same approach extended into the cafe interiors.

Guided by a “minimum intervention” and “zero damage” renovation strategy, Tant A Temps Design made every new addition detachable and reversible, which allowed the building’s original features to remain untouched.

In the cafe, the furniture is suspended from wooden beams or arranged around columns to avoid direct contact with the original structures.

Tant A Temps Design also created tables, chairs and display cabinets with designs that draw from elements of the ancient building framework, such as the beams, columns and dougong brackets.

Lightweight and prefabricated materials and modular systems were used throughout the space.

For the main colour palette, Tant A Temps Design chose light green hues complemented by gold accents.

“The purpose of choosing this colour scheme is to restore the visual characteristics of Tang architecture – robust, imposing and richly coloured,” the studio explained.

“Abandoning the rigid replication of ancient architecture, it extracts and reshapes the spiritual core of Tang and Song aesthetics through a restrained colour palette and minimalist structural language, creating a serene and elegant atmosphere that highly matches the cultural temperament of the Stele Forest.”

An integrated functional island was designed to function as the central bar counter.

All modern utility systems, including air conditioning, water, electricity, lighting and exhausts, were concealed and integrated into the top and bottom of the bar counter.

This is consistent with the studio’s commitment to preserving the heritage building while giving it a contemporary, functional upgrade.

“This forms a functional system that is both independent of the original building structure and seamlessly integrated into the historical environment, setting a new paradigm for the adaptive reuse of similar cultural heritage buildings,” said the studio.

The cafe is part of a 220-square-metre development that also includes a rest area, a retail zone and a stone-rubbing workshop that serves as a history learning centre.

According to Tant A Temps Design, the project has transformed a dormant historical building into an accessible and interactive cultural space.

Led by founder Wei Chen, Tant A Temps Design is an interior design practice based in Xi’an.

Elsewhere in China, Linehouse has completed the interiors of the Jen hotel in Hangzhou and Keiji Ashizawa designed an “open and inviting retail space” in the historic building in Shanghai.

#8969. red corrugated metal and pine plywood wrap czech village house’s extension

in nečín village, facha architekti renovates a converted pigsty and weekend cabin with a self-built timber extension that expands living spaces toward a stepped larch terrace.

LINKA News edited by christina vergopoulou November 16, 2026 4 min

Located on the edge of the village of Nečín in the Příbram region of the Czech Republic, House With a Red Addition is the renovation and extension of a compact family residence by Facha architekti. Originally built as a single-story pigsty and subsequently topped with a weekend cabin before becoming a permanent home, the structure retains visible markers of its incremental growth. Rather than unifying the building under a single envelope, the studio designed the new addition as a distinct architectural layer, defined by its sharp geometric form and a ventilated facade clad in red corrugated metal sheets.

The timber-framed extension expands the primary living zone toward the garden while relocating the main entrance and integrating built-in storage. On the west elevation, a large sliding window connects the living room to a larch terrace featuring wide seating steps and a retractable textile awning. Shifting the entrance into the new volume enabled a comprehensive reconfiguration of the raised ground floor, allowing for an enlarged bathroom finished in cement-based plaster and a redesigned kitchen. While the basement and attic were left largely intact, the original volume was thermally insulated, fitted with new timber windows, reroofed in corrugated metal, and upgraded with an air-to-water heat pump. Inside, pine plywood lines both the interior walls of the extension and custom-built furniture, paired with natural linoleum flooring and a rotating wood-burning stove. Consistent with Facha architekti’s hands-on methodology, the architects constructed the timber structure, metal cladding, and interior joinery directly alongside the clients.

#8968. Extra Skin? 9 Exercises for A Sagging Neck

We’re not in love with the term “turkey neck” — it’s just extra skin.

If you don’t want to learn to love the extra chin you’re in (though we wish you would!), you can perform some exercises that may tighten your neck muscles.

Though some swear these moves work, there’s no research backing them up, and they can’t zap away extra flowy skin.

Instead, they’re more likely to help strengthen the muscles underneath loose neck skin. Unfortunately, skin removal is usually accomplished with more intense methods, like surgery.

However, these popular neck exercises are simple enough for a test drive and may help tone your neck muscles naturally.

Exercise may be possible to tighten up a turkey neck, but it doesn’t eliminate loose skin like surgery or lasers.

Yes. Certain cosmetic products and procedures — especially surgery — improve loose neck skin the best. These include surgical neck lifts, lasers, Botox, and certain neck creams.

Surgery and other cosmetic methods for turkey neck can offer impressive results.

Are you not into cosmetic procedures or surgery? Neck-toning exercises and facial yoga movements may offer some improvement. However, loose skin is generally not tightened naturally.

Loose neck skin is normal (and honestly v common).

Still, these simple moves may result in toned neck muscles. Just be careful so you don’t wind up with an actual pain in the neck. If you can, it’s best to chat with a healthcare professional first.

#8967. Foster + Partners creates Area worktable for today's office

Foster + Partners Industrial Design aimed to bring expressive and functional workplace design together in its modular Area table system, created with Spanish furniture brand Kettal.

Designed to be durable and adaptable, Area combines aluminium columns, a panoply of tabletop options and concealed power.

The aluminium columns anchor the design, serving as both structural support and discreet container for power cables and electrical components.

Available in three diameters – 90, 160 or 450 millimetres – and either anodised or powder-coated finishes, they also bring customisable personality to the worktable.

The tabletops, meanwhile, come in shapes ranging from round to triangular and rhomboid and materials including timber, linoleum, melamine and Fenix. For larger conference or feature tables, terrazzo or marble are also options.

“Area is a collection of durable, expressive elements that define workstations and gathering points within a space to support both individual and collaborative work,” said Foster + Partners head of industrial design Mike Holland.

“The development of Area involved finding the right balance between structural performance, flexibility and visual simplicity,” he continued.

“The system needed to accommodate a wide variety of tabletop configurations and working arrangements, while integrating the technical infrastructure required in contemporary workplaces.”

The Area system can be accessorised with lighting or fabric screen dividers, the infrastructure for which is built into the table. Screen dividers attach magnetically at designed points, with lighting used in combination or mounted independently.

Cables are hidden underneath the tabletop within a J-profile aluminium beam that also provides structural support, while concealed grommets provide access to plug sockets and USB-C connections.

Holland told Dezeen that designing these accessories so they could function seamlessly across a range of tabletop configurations was the key challenge of the design process for Area, alongside achieving the desired proportions and textures for the aluminium columns.

To realise their vision for the expansive system, the design team undertook extensive prototyping, including using both one-to-one and full-scale models and augmented reality (AR).

“Working with full-scale models, augmented reality and 3D printing allowed us to understand the relationship between the different components and how they would function together in real working environments,” said Holland.

“This approach was particularly important in refining the columns, assessing their proportions, and adapting the surface texture pattern at full scale. It also allowed us to evolve the design from wider diameters into more elegant and efficient forms.”

He said that working with models and AR also allowed manufacturer Kettal to engage in the design process and contribute ideas.

“Collaboration is at the heart of our approach, and we believe it is fundamental to achieving the highest-quality results,” said Holland.

Area was designed for the contemporary workplace, said Holland, where flexible and hybrid working have made the office primarily a place for collaboration and connection, and where the table’s modularity and adaptability allow it to evolve as needs change.

“As designers, we are interested in the points of interaction between people and buildings,” said Holland. “At the heart of industrial design lies the creation of these touchpoints through which people experience space.”

“In the workplace, furniture plays a vital role in shaping how people engage with their environment, influencing how they occupy, navigate and connect with the spaces around them,” Holland concluded.

Part of the architecture firm Foster + Partners, Foster + Partners Industrial Design started by creating site-specific furniture, fixtures and fittings for the company’s buildings and over the last 50 years have expanded to more stand-alone commercial products.

Some of its recent designs include the Join plywood furniture collection, Ori bird feeders and Datum porcelain tableware.

#8966. sanrivatti ONE takes the forward lean of motorcycle racing into hypercar design

inspired by the physical immediacy of motorcycle riding, the apex position moves the driver forward in the cockpit, challenging conventional assumptions about visibility, control, and the experience of speed.

Sanrivatti ONE, the debut hypercar of the company, is developed around a driving architecture that places the driver in a forward-leaning, head-forward position. The vehicle brings together an experimental approach to cockpit ergonomics and a lightweight, naturally aspirated performance platform.

Τhe company’s proprietary Apex Position moves the driver forward and upright compared with the reclined position found in most hypercars. Inspired by the physical immediacy of riding a high-performance motorcycle, the arrangement aims to create a closer relationship between the driver’s body, the vehicle, and the circuit. According to Sanrivatti, the position provides a more open field of vision, a heightened perception of acceleration and cornering, and a more precise understanding of the car’s placement on track.

The Dutch automotive company introduces the Apex Position and influences the relationship between the driver, cockpit, steering system, pedals, and surrounding bodywork. The intention is to make driving a more physical experience, where the driver feels more directly connected to the movements of the vehicle.

Sanrivatti says that the position provides 3.2 times more of the circuit in view at Corner Three at Silverstone, compared with a selection of ten hypercars and track cars. The company also reports a vertical field of view of 28 degrees, against 15.5 degrees for its benchmark hypercar.

The approach has also informed the exterior proportions of the ONE. Its low, elongated body features a sweeping upper line, a single-piece canopy, and pronounced through-body air tunnels. Sanrivatti cites the peregrine falcon in a high-speed dive and the precision of modern fighter aircraft as references for the design. The silhouette appears shaped around the driver’s forward position, with the cockpit integrated into a body that emphasizes directional movement and aerodynamic expression.

Sanrivatti targets an 800 hp output from a naturally aspirated 5.5-liter Judd V10, paired with a six-speed Hewland sequential gearbox and rear-wheel drive. A carbon-fiber monocoque forms the structural foundation, while the targeted dry weight is 1,100 kg.

The company also lists a target torque of 700 Nm and a projected maximum speed of 330 km/h. All these figures remain provisional and subject to development, testing, and validation.

The choice of a naturally aspirated V10 and sequential transmission points toward a driving experience centered on direct mechanical feedback. The ONE proposes an interpretation of contemporary performance that places physical engagement and driver perception at the forefront.

#8965. Pepper & Well designs bathroom that mimics concrete architecture of Paul Couch house

Melbourne-based studio Pepper & Well took cues from crisscrossing concrete walls and ceiling beams when designing Lumeah, a new en-suite for a house by celebrated architect Paul Couch.

Located in Macedon, central Victoria, the linear single-storey house was completed in 2006 by the late Couch, who passed away earlier this year.

When new owners bought the property in 2018, they felt the layout and finishes of the main bathroom didn’t meet the standards of the rest of the house.

They asked Pepper & Well to upgrade it and make it more accessible.

“There was an opportunity to make the space more comfortable and practical as they aged,” said lead architect Andy Dal Pozzo.

The previous layout included a WC, an enclosed shower and a step-in plunge pool, all within a space just 3.5 metres long.

Pepper & Well’s scheme removed the plunge, allowing space for a larger WC and for an open shower to be built in place of the old frosted-glass enclosure.

The defining move was the addition of a cast-concrete element that partitions the toilet and shower areas.

This incorporates an informal bench, allowing for seated showers if preferred.

The geometry of this element clearly references the house’s exposed concrete structure, a rhythmic arrangement of concrete beams over concrete walls.

“Our approach began with understanding the logic of Paul’s work,” explained Dal Pozzo.

“We wanted the renovation to share the original architecture’s material honesty and clarity, while remaining recognisable as a new contribution,” he said.

A change in floor surface marks the junction between old and new.

While most of the room features the bluestone flooring installed 20 years ago, the toilet and shower have a surface of crazy-paved slate.

The stone is the same Mintaro Brown Back slate that Couch installed in the bathroom of his own house, Toolern Vale.

“Laid in crazy paving beside the retained bluestone, it introduces a distinct texture with a direct connection to Paul’s work,” said Dal Pozzo.

The rest of the room was left largely intact, including the solid timber doors and the vanity unit spanning the opposite wall.

There are subtle correlations between the two sides of the room, so as not to make the new insertion feel disparate. For instance, a glass screen matches the height of the mirror opposite.

The shower also includes a stainless-steel handrail that doubles as a towel rail, matching the rest of the bathroom fixtures.

“The scale of the commission demanded close attention to every decision, from the arrangement of the room to the meeting of two stones,” added Dal Pozzo.

“By revealing the original fabric, retaining what worked and introducing a few carefully resolved elements, we sought to give the clients a bathroom that would serve them into the future and continue the architectural story of their home.”

Lumeah is shortlisted for bathroom of the year in Dezeen Awards 2026.

Other projects in this category include Kan Atelier’s design for the William King Apartment, a residence in a 1950s block in Athens, which won the public vote.

#8964. Nopales Benefits: Why You Might Add Cactus to Your Diet

Looking at a cactus with its threatening spikes and tough skin, you might not immediately think, “Yep, that’s a thing I could eat.” But guess what? Some forms of cacti are edible, tasty, and quite good for you!

Check out why it might be a good idea to pal around with nopales, the pads of the prickly pear cactus.

The nopal cactus, also known as the prickly pear or the opuntia, is a shrub-like, flowering cactus native to parts of Mexico, Arizona, the Mediterranean, Australia, and other desert regions. It might be recognized by its multitude of connected pads with flowering blooms. (A pad in bloom looks a little like a flat, green paw.)

Nopales flowers are filled with a viscous, seeded substance often used in jams, jellies, pies, cakes, and other sweets. But the stems, leaves, and entire pad (with spines removed, obvs) are also edible. Traditional Mexican preparations include boiling, grilling, and sautéing.

Science is still examining the possible benefits of nopales, so some touted wellness perks are fairly tentative. Here’s a look at what we know about these desert fruits.

Almost any time you see bright colors in edible fruits, it’s a sign they contain antioxidants. This is def true for Nopales!

Older studies have found that the fruit inside their flowers is rich in antioxidants like ascorbic acid, phenolics, and a mixture of betacyanin and betaxanthin. These compounds help fight inflammation by kicking harmful free radicals out of your cells.

Since they combat inflammation, the antioxidants in prickly pear could improve joint mobility. In a 2020 study, people who drank 3 ounces of prickly pear juice daily for 8 weeks had better range of motion and greater ease with daily activities than a control group who drank a placebo.

Research suggests nopales may help steady blood sugar. A 2014 study found that people with type 2 diabetes who ate nopales with a high-carb breakfast had significantly lower blood sugar and insulin levels compared to those who didn’t. However, this study only included 14 participants.

In 2019, a larger systematic review assessed the fruit’s potential for blood sugar regulation. While it found insufficient evidence to support using nopales to reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes, the authors noted it might significantly reduce blood glucose levels.

Showing your liver some love might involve adding nopales (or a glass of nopal juice) to your diet. According to research from 2023, this has to do with prickly pear’s effects on triglycerides. By helping reduce triglyceride accumulation, nopales could relieve stress on the liver.

Whether you’ve overdone it on booze or are down with a stomach bug, it’s important to rehydrate with a drink that contains electrolytes. Consider prickly pear juice as your back-on-the-wagon beverage. It’s got potassium, magnesium, and calcium to help rebalance your electrolyte levels.

If you can track down fresh nopales where you live, cooking it yourself is a fun (if somewhat complicated) way to take advantage of its benefits. If not, look for prickly pear products, such as juices, being sure to check for added sugars.

You can also take a supplement. Nopales supplements typically contain 500-650 milligrams (mg) per day.

While a prickly pear smoothie or nopales salad can be a healthy addition to your diet, consuming this cactus fruit may have some less-than-desirable side effects, like:

If you’re new to nopales, take it slow at first to see how your body responds.

Don’t let the “prickly” in prickly pear keep you away from this desert gem. When prepared correctly, nopales are unique, nutritious food. Check ’em out when your fruit basket needs something a little different.

#8963. B2 Architecture turns North Korean defector testimonies into Prague exhibition

Photography by Radek Šrettr Úlehla

B2 Architecture has created the Life Behind the Walls exhibition in Prague, using a maze of red timber frames and translucent fabric to explore life in North Korea.

The 1,500-square-metre exhibition takes visitors from a bright, interactive installation designed around a children’s book to a darkened gallery featuring portraits and testimonies from North Korean defectors.

B2 Architecture divided the installation into two contrasting environments. The first features a grid of red-painted timber beams, with large sheets of red and pink fabric suspended between the frames to create semi-transparent walls.

The structure forms a maze that visitors can explore, with glimpses of other rooms and activities visible through the fabric.

Illustrated panels, games and interactive activities are fitted into the structure, while photographs by photographer Michal Huniewicz show North Korea as it is presented to the outside world.

Children are encouraged to navigate the maze independently and stop to draw, write and complete activities as they move through the installation.

The displays are based on Tota lítá, a children’s book by North Korean studies scholar and writer Nina Špitálníková, which explains the principles of totalitarianism in language that is accessible to younger readers.

“Children are often given very little space within exhibition formats,” B2 Architecture told Dezeen. “This project consciously challenges that convention.”

The atmosphere changes as visitors pass between two walls displaying photographs of the border between North Korea and China by photographer Tim Franco.

Beyond this threshold, the playful red maze gives way to a dark gallery. This contains black display structures with portraits and personal accounts of people who escaped North Korea, alongside stories of those who did not survive its regime.

Tall, translucent fabric panels printed with shadowy human figures were arranged throughout the space, creating silhouettes that overlap with the portraits displayed behind them.

In a central room, a monumental statue of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un stands on a raised plinth, surrounded by spotlights and theatrical mist.

The temporary installation was constructed using lightweight, modular timber beams and stretched textiles, allowing it to be assembled and dismantled efficiently.

The timber structure was retained for use in another project, while the textiles and flooring were passed on to several theatres for reuse.

Prague-based B2 Architecture was founded by architect Barbara Bencová in 2012 and works across residential and commercial architecture, interiors and public spaces.

Other projects by the studio featured on Dezeen include the DDB Prague office, which features an anamorphic optical illusion that makes the advertising agency’s logo appear complete from a particular viewpoint.

Photography by Radek Šrettr Úlehla

#8962. Eight highlights from this year's Sharjah Architecture Triennial

The third Sharjah Architecture Triennial focuses on the myriad ways architecture can be understood through the lens of anthropology. Here are our highlights from the event, including installations and exhibitions.

Curated by anthropologist Vyjayanthi Rao, this year’s edition was centred on the theme Architecture Otherwise: Building Civic Infrastructure for Collective Futures.

Rao said the 2026 Sharjah Architecture Triennial, which takes place over five months, will invite discourse about the different ways cities and urban life can be imagined.

“Though I’m not an architect, I’m literally talking to students day in and day out about how they see the world, and how that translates into the practice,” Rao told Dezeen.

“Being an academic, you’re always asked to define yourself in terms of your discipline,” she continued. “It doesn’t make sense to limit yourself, especially when you are in the practice of life.”

“You’re learning from people about the ways in which they live – that’s what I do as an anthropologist, and I think that’s what a lot of architects do because they’re inspired to build for people and the places that they inhabit and thrive in.”

Read on for eight highlights from this year’s Sharjah Architecture Triennial.

Artist Curry J Hackett created this draping shelter spanning the width of the Old Al Jubail Vegetable Market in homage to the Black community in Virginia’s Prince Edward County, which created improvised learning spaces when schools closed during the Civil Rights Movement.

Videos play in the former stalls at either end of the fabric enclosure, screening archival images of the period, as well as images of Rosenwald Schools – the community-building initiative that established thousands of schools for Black children in the South.

“Rather than integrate, schools closed for five years, and leading up to that, schools were dealing with a lot of overcrowding,” Hackett told Dezeen. “The county begrudgingly funded ‘tar paper shacks’, which were shoddy, demoralising structures, to ease overcrowding, and that’s what you’re seeing interpreted here,” he continued.

“Interspersed sonically and visually throughout the installation is a mashing up of the local story of my home town in Virginia with the regional story of the Rosenwald Schools in the South – their architectural rethinking of materials and retelling the history.”

Research and construction studio Abari showcased a tent-like structure made from a bamboo frame, which was limited in size due to difficulties with material regulations.

The structure is one module of a larger pavilion that was constructed in Nepal, designed as a travelling venue to host bamboo weaving workshops.

“We were not able to create an installation here in the UAE, partly because Abari’s work is based on building with bamboo, and the difficulty with this project was that the global supply chain and its regulations could not be met within the timeframe,” said Rao.

“What you see here is one repeatable module of a pavilion that is currently moving within different communities in Nepal – we improvised and decided Sharjah would travel to Nepal, and we’d just have a piece of it here in this exhibition.”

Drawing upon her fieldwork in Sharjah, Palestinian architect Samar Halloum designed a brick pavilion that was shaded overhead by a draping fabric canopy.

In reference to the historical public drinking-water structures in the Gulf region, Sabeel Negotiated features a water fountain and wooden stools for people to gather around.

According to Rao, the strikes by Iran on countries in the Middle East in February disrupted brick supply in the United Arab Emirates, so Halloum redesigned the pavilion with cloth-filled bricks.

“One of the shortages was bricks because they come from Saudi Arabia, and the factory stopped producing bricks,” said Rao. “There were some leftover bales of cloth from another installation, so Halloum used those bales and cast them in resin, so you’ll see some of the bricks in the installation are actually made of cloth.”

History as Repair: Documenting Karachi by Kishwar Rizvi

This exhibition by art historian Kishwar Rizvi explores how colonised communities in Karachi, Pakistan, took ownership of their urban environment by adapting architectural styles, from European classicism to Mughal-inspired ornament.

Through maps, photographs, sketches and interviews, it aims to shine a light on an architectural history at risk of being forgotten.

The exhibition argues for the protection of colonial-era buildings in Karachi, which are under threat of demolition due to neglect.

Patch-Time by Hiba Bou Akar, Mohamad Hafeda and Nathalie Harb

The Patch-Time installation is a collaboration between researchers Hiba Bou Akar and Mohamad Hafeda and artist Nathalie Harb that explores the displacement of people in Lebanon, from the 1970s to the present day, through the materials used to protect and repair homes.

In workshops organised by Lebanese non-profit Ahla Fawda, displaced women crocheted tarpaulin, sand-bag cloth and sheeting into panels that form a canopy displayed in a courtyard at the triennial’s Al Qasimiyah School venue.

Underneath the canopy, a table made from breeze blocks, wood and a central mirror displays fabric artwork and the stories of women and children affected by war.

“We worked on two levels: one that is the collective, and one that is more of the individual, looking at how people shelter their home through war adversity and displacement,” said Harb. “We asked [the women] what their relationship to their home was, and in the pieces, you see how it changes from generation to generation with their relationship to material.”

After Night There is Nothing by Mohamad Nahleh and Ozayr Saloojee

Architect Mohamad Nahleh and architecture professor Ozayr Saloojee designed a giant globe of the night sky and split it into three parts, which were scattered across different locations at the triennale.

The outer shells of the curved structures are wrapped in thatch, while the interiors feature vinyl surfaces with designs showing man-made military objects in the sky reimagined as creature-like constellations.

“This is ‘night sky optimism’ – optimism through catastrophe,” said Nahleh. “The night sky we are talking about in this project is not the sky of beautiful stars and constellations, but the contemporary sky filled with drones, satellites, rockets and missiles that are changing the way we understand the sky above us.”

“We have noticed in our research that, especially in geographies witnessing prolonged violence, these objects are producing new mythical creatures,” he continued. “We think of these creatures as ones that attempt to tame the military brightness that is populating the sky around us.”

Kuwaiti designer Badriyah Alsalem plotted 41 medieval Arabic poetic names for the sun as cut-outs on the astronomical graph that forms a circular canopy over her pavilion, As the Sun Rests.

Forming patterns of shadow in the sand below, three of the suns were embroidered in red, depicting the sharaq rising sun, saqa’a noon sun and gharab setting sun, while markers on the ground show where these canopy highlights will fall on different dates during the triennial.

“If you look up, you see the static data visualisation, and if you look down, it is animated by the sun itself, so it becomes an analogue device to read this historical data,” said Alsalem.

Lalla Alwyia Khalwa by Ziad Jamaleddine, Makram el Kadi, Iheb Guermazi and Beya Othmani

Situated on Sharjah’s Al Khan Open Beach, Lalla Alwyia Khalwa is an installation designed as a place for reflection away from the busy city, dedicated to the saint Lalla Alwyia Kasserine.

Dried plants form a grid of columns on a raised platform for visitors to walk through. Stone slabs on the floor mark places of pause, and a metal stool provides a reflective space to listen to the accompanying sound installation.

“We chose the beach because it is already a space for retreat, so this is a retreat inside a retreat,” said the design team, Ziad Jamaleddine, Makram el Kadi, Iheb Guermazi and Beya Othmani.

“We carved a series of spaces – one for prayer, one for sitting, and a courtyard to enjoy the sky.”

Sharjah Architecture Triennial 2026 takes place from 14 November 2026 to 14 April 2027 at various locations across Sharjah, UAE. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

#8961. PLANTIQUE gives houseplants a little robot companion to express their needs

designed by karan aneja, the device turns soil moisture readings into expressive facial feedback, giving houseplants a playful way to communicate their needs.

PLANTIQUE by Karan Aneja is an interactive plant-monitoring device that translates environmental readings into expressive visual feedback. Combining a capacitive soil moisture sensor with a small OLED display, the orange, robot-like object gives houseplants a recognizable interface, replacing numerical readings with animated facial expressions.

The project explores how emotional visualization and familiar forms of communication might encourage people to pay closer attention to the living things around them. Plants constantly respond to changes in their environment, but these processes are largely invisible to the people who care for them. Soil moisture, light exposure, and other environmental conditions can influence their growth, yet understanding when a plant needs attention often requires observation and experience. PLANTIQUE approaches this communication, turning sensor information into a more approachable everyday interaction.

The device takes the form of a compact character with a rounded rectangular body, a flexible-looking neck connection, and three antenna-like protrusions extending from its head. Its black OLED screen displays turquoise facial expressions, giving the object a recognizable personality. A slender capacitive soil moisture sensor extends from its base into the soil, allowing the device to monitor moisture levels while remaining integrated into the pot of the plant.

PLANTIQUE’s changing expressions offer an immediate indication of the conditions detected by the sensor, making technical information easier to interpret without requiring users to understand the underlying measurements. The device introduces different character identities, including Zest, Sunny, and Sprout, each presented through variations in color and facial expression.

#8960. Ultimate Guide to 4A Hair: Care Tips, Styles, and Maintenance

Understanding your hair type is key to achieving healthy, luscious curls. Hair types range from 1 to 4 — straight, wavy, curly, and coily — with type 4 being the curliest. Type 4A hair has a fine texture and loose curl pattern, forming springy coils that need special care to stay healthy and vibrant.

Knowing your hair type helps determine the best hair care routine. Caring for 4A hair is essential, whether you’re dealing with dryness or breakage or want to define your curls.

Let’s dive into the world of 4A hair and discover how to keep those curls popping.

Alright, curl friends, let’s break it down. Hair type falls into four main categories:

Now, Type 4 hair is where things get seriously curly and coily. Within this category, we’ve got subtypes A, B, and C,

which refer to the width and density of your curls.

So, what’s the deal with 4A hair? 4A hair is the queen of the fine, loose curl pattern. It forms tight, springy coils that are like tiny, perfect S-shapes. These curls are less dense than their 4B and 4C cousins, making them more defined and delicate. Think of 4A hair as the Goldilocks of coily hair — not too tight, not too loose, but just right.

Your hair is unique and gorgeous, but it requires a bit of extra TLC to keep it looking its best. Here’s a straightforward guide to keeping your 4A hair moisturized, healthy, and thriving:

4A hair tends to be dry as its coily structure makes it difficult for natural oils to travel down the hair shaft. Keeping it moisturized is essential, so incorporate a good leave-in conditioner into your daily shampooing routine. Use deep conditioning treatments weekly to replenish moisture and strengthen your curls.

Don’t forget scalp care, too! For maximum hydration, look for products with ingredients like shea butter, coconut oil, and glycerin.

4A hair is prone to tangles, so detangle gently to avoid breakage. Use a wide-tooth comb or your fingers to work through knots carefully. Start from the ends and work your way up to the roots, and always detangle when your hair is wet and coated with conditioner to provide slip and minimize damage.

Heat styling tools can cause significant damage to 4A hair, leading to dryness, breakage, and loss of curl pattern. Minimize the use of blow dryers, flat irons, and curling wands. If you use heat, always apply a heat protectant spray first to shield your hair from high temperatures.

Pro tip: To maintain the health of your curls, opt for air-drying or styles that don’t require heat.

Protective styles like braids, twists, and buns can help reduce manipulation and minimize breakage. These styles tuck away your ends, protecting them from friction and environmental damage.

Cotton pillowcases cause friction, which leads to frizz and breakage, especially for 4A hair. Switching to satin or silk pillowcases instead helps mai

ntain your curl pattern and prevent tangles.

Regular trims are crucial for keeping 4A hair healthy and preventing split ends from traveling up the hair shaft. Aim to trim your hair every 8-12 weeks to remove damaged ends and keep your curls looking fresh and vibrant.

Yes, 4A hair is curly and falls under the coily category. It features tight, springy curls that form an S-shape.

To determine your hair type, look at the curl pattern, texture, and density. 4A hair has a loose curl pattern with fine, springy coils, while 4B and 4C hair have tighter curls. 3C hair is curly but not as tight as Type 4.

Washing once a week or every two weeks is generally sufficient for 4A hair. Overwashing can strip the hair of its natural oils.

Regular trims every 8-12 weeks help keep 4A hair healthy by removing split ends and preventing breakage.

Taking care of your 4A hair isn’t rocket science, but it does need a little know-how and the right tools.

Love those natural curls — keep them hydrated, avoid excessive heat, and give them some nighttime TLC.
