#8959. Casa Mouda opens Lagos gallery to promote design in Nigeria

Papa Omotayo, Gemma Sfeir and Nifemi Marcus-Bello have helped design two spaces in Lagos for the local creative studio Casa Mouda to host exhibitions that promote design in West Africa.

Casa Mouda’s initiative includes the launch of an exhibition to mark the opening of two spaces in Lagos – aiMe Gallery at Eko Hotel and aiMe Concept on Eko Atlantic.

AiMe Gallery was redesigned by Lagos-based architect Omotayo at the entrance to the hotel’s conference centre, while aiMe Concept was designed with interior designer Sfeir and designer Marcus-Bello in a storefront in the larger Eko Atlantic development.

Both spaces feature exposed concrete walls and columns with touches of warmth, including an earthen bar and screen in aiMe Gallery.

Casa Mouda founder Caline Chagoury Moudaber said that the spaces, together, were designed to highlight the work done by designers in Lagos.

“As we began to conceive our first chapter of Casa Mouda, we knew we needed to start by recognizing some of the people who had already built so much of its foundation,” said Chagoury Moudaber.

“There are incredible designers producing on the continent that have done extraordinary work, often taking on alone what usually takes an entire industry elsewhere.”

The inaugural exhibitions include designers from Lagos, but also those who have chosen to work in the city from abroad.

Among the latter group is American designer Germane Barnes, who showcased his wooden Corona Chair, which features inverted pyramidal legs, and his take on a peacock chair, both produced in Lagos in collaboration with Casa Mouda.

Beyond his contribution to the interior layout, which includes permanent seating for the hospitality at aiMe Concept, Marcus-Bello showcased his LM stools and M2 shelves. The works showcase the production possible in Lagos, but also a more modern, minimalist angle for Marcus-Bello, who is known for his massive metal collectible design pieces.

“Nifemi Marcus-Bello has been quietly doing the legwork to set up real pathways for production for years,” said Chagoury Moudaber.

On the more craft-oriented side, the collection showcased works in bronze and wood by craftsman Jean Servais Somian, also produced in collaboration with Casa Mouda.

Servais Somian’s work includes an armoire with gridded screen wooden doors, a console with stacked oval shelves, stools in wood with painted recesses that have a graphic appearance and textural cast bronze stools and side tables. It is an impressive array showcasing the craftsman’s range.

French studio Hall Haus showcased its metal basketball hoops and chairs, a blend of African aesthetics with Parisian urban ephemera, reflecting the cross-cultural background of the studio’s members.

Meanwhile, Moroccan designer Hajar Daide showcased a mix of delicate Nigerian woven wood techniques with lush blue Moroccan fabrics for her Friction Bench.

Atmosphere was top of mind for the designers, and Casa Mouda worked with US musician Malloy James to create custom speakers at the entryway for aiMe Gallery, while aiMe Concept features a listening station.

The spaces have also been set up to further promote craft in the region through display and retail, such as textiles, bags and other smaller items such as jewellery.

“The designers who have forged the way are sharing information on what they have learned; the ones new to this area of production are bringing new techniques and perspectives,” said Chagoury Moudaber.

“It has been an incredibly collaborative, generous, and inspiring process – and we are only just beginning.”

Other recent design showcases include the inaugural Walker Design Triennial in Minnesota and Danish design initiative The Mindcraft Project, curated by Christian + Jade.

#8958. Pucker Up! How to Heal Cracked Lip Corners Fast

Smiling for selfies should be fun, not painful! If cracked lip corners or angular cheilitis make it hard to smile, eat, or kiss, don’t worry. Check out these tips to heal those cracks quickly. With some care and good habits, you’ll have pain-free, makeout-ready lips in no time. Say goodbye to angular cheilitis and hello to a happier smile!

The first step to healing your cracked lip corners quickly is to lock in any moisture. Reach for a product dermatologists call an occlusive, which creates a protective barrier that prevents your lip corners from getting drier. Vaseline, Aquafor, or CeraVe ointment are common occlusives that will help reduce cracking.

Dab a little coconut oil, olive oil, or fragrance-free moisturizer on the corners of your lips daily after you shower. Make it a daily habit, but don’t go overboard. A little dab will do. Allow your skin’s natural oils to build back up as the cracking fades. Bonus tip: Add the occlusive lip barrier after moisturizing.

Locking in moisture only works if you have enough moisture, so staying hydrated is key! Keep a refillable water bottle with you as your trusty sidekick. Sip on plain water throughout the day, or jazz it up with a splash of cucumber or another non-acidic flavor. Pro tip: Avoid lemon juice, which can irritate and sting sensitive skin.

Bonus: Staying hydrated will help your raw lip corners heal quicker and improve your skin’s overall health.

Have you noticed that moisture is a common theme here? Lend your lips a humid hand by sleeping with a humidifier beside your bed. Adding moisture to the air is especially helpful for your cracked lips during the winter or in hot, dry climates. Think about popping a small humidifier in your workspace or wherever you spend the most time.

It might seem like a quick fix to lick your lips to keep them moist, but that can make things worse. Saliva evaporates quickly, leaving a sticky residue that can attract bacteria and lead to infection. So, keep your tongue away from your lips and remember this: “Licking your lips will cause them to lickety-split.”

Whether from frigid cold or dry heat, your skin can lose water rapidly, causing cracking, flaking, discoloration, or swelling. So avoid jumping from a sweltering afternoon at the beach into a freezing cold movie theater.

Also, skip the hot showers or cold plunges for a bit. These types of rapid temperature changes will quickly dry out your lip corners. Bonus tip: Your lips can take a beating from the sun, so find a lip balm with SPF protection.

If your cracked lip corners don’t improve or become especially painful or swollen in a few days, it’s time to visit a board-certified dermatologist. If left untreated, angular cheilitis can last for years, leaving your lips discolored or scarred.

FYI: Angular cheilitis might not appear as clearly in people with darker skin. Instead of turning red, the affected skin may look pale and have a darker border.

Remember that lickety-split mantra? It’s for real. Saliva can get deposited in the corners of your lips for many reasons, like drooling, smoking, or sleeping with your mouth open due to some sniffles. Bacteria grows in those little saliva pools, triggering an inflammatory response that causes your lip corners to get irritated and crack.

Following these tips will make your lips feel better in about a week. Really bad cases of angular cheilitis can take a few weeks. Avoid smoking and eat a balanced diet to get faster results.

As mentioned above, Vaseline and other occlusives help create a protective barrier over the cracked lip corners, which helps the healing process.

You might have woken up with cracked lip corners, but you won’t be able to get rid of them overnight. Be patient and follow the tips above!

Say goodbye to painful cracked lip corners in about a week with these easy tips:

Talk to a dermatologist for customized care if your lip corners become red, swollen, or more painful after a few days.

#8957. Shisuo Design Office creates "surreal" rural house in China using salvaged steel

Jiang Deng Lu is a house in rural Anhui designed by Chinese studio Shisuo Design Office using stainless-steel offcuts salvaged from the client’s own factory.

Described by Shisuo Design Office as a “surreal rural house”, the compact building is raised partially on stilts to look as though it is floating above its sloped riverside site.

It sits beside the client’s ancestral home and serves as both a memorial for his late father and a separate dwelling where his elderly mother can host visiting relatives.

“The client wanted to build a house beside the old family home, providing a comfortable place for his mother and relatives to gather and share meals during holidays,” Shisuo Design Office told Dezeen.

“But beyond this practical need, there was a deeper emotional connection. The old house was left by his father, while the new one represented his own way of creating new memories for the family,” it continued.

“We hoped the house would bring the family together more often, beyond just festive occasions.”

Jiang Deng Lu’s proportions were determined by the recycled stainless steel offcuts and unused windows salvaged for the project by the client, who is the owner of a stainless steel factory.

“The building’s geometry was strictly reverse-engineered from these salvaged materials,” said Shisuo Design Office.

“Instead of imposing a predetermined architectural form, we meticulously measured and mapped these specific surplus components. The building’s precise dimensions, roof pitches, and structural envelope were entirely reverse-engineered from this salvaged inventory,” added the studio.

“The resulting structure starkly contrasts the client’s modern, lightweight metal industry with the heavy, rooted legacy of his father’s masonry, translating familial love into a rigorous tectonic language,” the studio said.

Externally, the house is wrapped in a full stainless-steel facade, which the studio said deliberately contrasts with “traditional rural vernacular”. This is punctured by the salvaged windows, positioned to frame views of the river.

It has a rectangular plan, with a balcony that is suspended over the river on one side.

Inside is a living space, which sits raised above a dining area accessed directly from the foyer. A bathroom and shower room sit off this dining space.

Interior finishes are pared-back, with stone flooring and white walls complementing the cool-toned exterior of the home. Wooden furnishings and greenery seen through the windows add warmth to the space.

According to Shisuo Design Office, the highlight of the interior is a nine-metre-long window that cantilevers 2.2 metres outward, providing shelter for the terrace below.

“The most distinctive feature is a nine-metre-long horizontal window facing east, overlooking a grove of trees planted by the client’s late father,” said the studio.

“For the client, these trees are more than a landscape; they hold personal memories of his father. We wanted to bring the grove into everyday life, rather than simply frame it as a view.”

Jiang Deng Lu is shortlisted in the rural house category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards, alongside projects including Casa Plaj by Extrastudio and Hata-Mazanka Guesthouses by YOD Group.

Another house featured on Dezeen with a distinctive metal facade is Bondi House, a two-storey, two-bedroom dwelling by Nick Kent Design in Sydney.

#8956. podcast: indian architects adapt building codes and restore soil through trust

the two conversations bring together seven indian practitioners to dissect the unseen negotiations of contemporary practice.

Continuing to explore how architecture tests alternative ways of living, the Room for Utopias podcast series, produced in collaboration with INDX|GLOBAL, presents its fourth feature. Following previous panel discussions in Paris that examined site listening and dismantled the myth of the signature style, this double feature examines the friction between rigid institutional frameworks and the human relationships required to realize a building. Hosted by designboom Managing Editor, Iñaki Laguardia, the two conversations bring together seven Indian practitioners to dissect the unseen negotiations of contemporary practice: challenging obsolete building codes, accepting material imperfection, and establishing interpersonal trust as an essential structural foundation.

Sumit Dhawan of Cityspace 82 Architects opens the seventh episode by addressing the friction between advancing construction capabilities and static regulatory frameworks in India. Dhawan observes that while digital design tools and fabrication methods upgrade continually, statutory building codes remain decades behind current practice. ‘Technology-based items are getting upgraded every year, but not our building bylaws… trust me, in India we are still using iPhone 1 with respect to building bylaws, and otherwise we’ve reached iPhone 18,‘ Dhawan states. To overcome these limitations, his studio actively questions statutory policies, demonstrating how spatial arguments can produce compliant habitable basements where rigid interpretations once banned them. Sachi Gupta of Synthesis contrasts this situation with the regulatory climate in the UK, where environmental performance standards update every six months, requiring studios to continually adjust technical assemblies to align with legal mandates.

Siddharth Talwar of STA+D directs attention toward the non-negotiable physical rules established by the terrain itself. Rather than rushing into excavation and foundation pours, Talwar proposes dedicating initial project phases to environmental site repair. ‘Can we spend the first few years ecologically restoring the land? Look at how the water is flowing… allow for that kind of restoration to happen so the land is strong enough to take the act of building,‘ Talwar explains. Arguing that existing structures represent the most sustainable spatial resource, Talwar rejects singular aesthetic branding in favor of adaptive reuse, leaving structures open to spontaneous future adjustments by the occupants who inhabit them.

Rashna Agarwal of Studio IAAD and Zoera, returning to the series after discussing material lifespans at Milan Design Week 2026, critiques the pursuit of hyper-polished environments that resist human touch. Agarwal explains that contemporary building requires dozens of simultaneous contributors, moving final decision-making away from an individual artistic ego toward project managers, cost consultants, and fabricators. ‘We’ve started making things just too perfect… I’m going to find an answer where there is some bit of imperfection… so that touch-me-not feel has to go away,‘ Agarwal says. By deliberately accommodating material variation and natural wear, spaces retain room to settle over time.

The physical consequences of these positions appear in unpolished, tactile assemblies. Instead of sealing rooms behind uniform white partitions and mirrored paneling, the studios prioritize materials that reveal how a structure comes together. Habitable subterranean levels cut into hard earth draw indirect light through sunken stone lightwells, where retaining walls built from local rubble stay exposed rather than concealed behind veneers. Unsealed stone floors, lime washes, and hand-cut timber joinery allow surfaces to take on patina through daily contact, while open swales cut directly into the ground channel seasonal runoff to nourish native groundcover rather than directing rainwater into enclosed storm pipes.

The eigth episode examines the intangible bonds that keep complex commissions together during execution. Jaskaran Singh of Fab Studio describes interpersonal trust as an unseen binder that unites the client’s capital investment with the studio’s technical and creative output. ‘Think of it like the invisible glue. In fact, it binds the entire thing together… Trust is really that bridge which joins these two risks and takes a project forward,‘ Singh explains. Ashmit Alag of Transform Design echoes this view, noting that client confidence directly influences operational efficiency: ‘There’s a saying that you build trust before you start building the walls. And if the trust is established, you’re not negotiating; rather, you’re all commonly moving towards the same goal.‘

When budget pressures, contractor delays, or site complications introduce friction, project members often withdraw into defensive positions. Parvez Alam of Synthesis notes that architects must maintain technical stewardship over the entire assembly to prevent work from deteriorating into compromised settlements. ‘When the trust dilution is happening… everybody’s trying to save their own interest… but as a captain, we have to take ownership. So we have to support everything that is happening and steer things towards a more collaborative team effort,‘ Alam remarks. Alag observes that while creative work naturally introduces unpredictability, clear communication and rigorous coordination keep design intent intact without alienating collaborators.

Both Singh and Alam conclude that enduring spatial design depends on understanding the emotional motives of the inhabitants rather than following surface-level image boards. Singh notes that clients often share digital references without knowing how to articulate their functional requirements, requiring architects to probe why an occupant responds to a particular volume or light condition. Alam explains that residential commissions typically span several years, during which project briefs expand into living documents that reflect shifting household routines and family milestones. For Alag, the ultimate indicator of spatial success is whether the architect remains welcome in the finished home during significant family events years after handover.

Across both panels, the conversations demonstrate that building alternative futures does not rely on imposing immaculate formal monuments. By questioning obsolete bylaws, rehabilitating raw land, accepting material imperfections, and anchoring execution in shared trust, these Indian practitioners show that the most resilient architecture grows from the patient work of daily collaboration.

guests: Sumit Dhawan (Cityspace 82 Architects | @cityspace82_architects), Sidharth Talwar (STA+D | @sidharthatalwar), Sachi Gupta (Synthesis | @synthesislondon), Rachna Agarwal (Studio IAAD | Zoera | @studio.iaad), Jaskaran Singh (Fab Studio | @fabinteriors_fabstudio), Ashmit Alag (Transform Design | @transform_design_studio), Parvez Alam (Synthesis | @synthesislondon)

in partnership with: AMICI | @amici_india; MARMO SOLUTIONS | @marmosolutionsindia; AGGLOTECH | @agglotech

## The Moment You Recline Into ANA "The Room" The flight attendant slides your suite door closed. You're somewhere over the Pacific, 35,000 feet above the ocean, enclosed in what ANA calls "The Room" — a fully private, floor-to-ceiling enclosed business class suite on a Boeing 777-300ER. The seat converts to a fully flat 78-inch bed. There's direct aisle access. The service is famously meticulous. And you're flying from New York to Tokyo in a product that rivals first class on most other carriers. This is not a fantasy. This is what 90,000 Virgin Atlantic Flying Club miles buys you on ANA's JFK → NRT route. ### The Math That Should Stop You Cold A one-way business class ticket on ANA between New York and Tokyo typically retails for **$6,000 to $12,000 in cash**. That's not a typo. Premium cabin trans-Pacific fares are genuinely that expensive, which is precisely why the ChooseFI community treats travel rewards as a core pillar of the FI lifestyle — you're unlocking experiences that would otherwise require years of extra saving. At 90,000 Virgin Atlantic miles for that same seat, your points are delivering **6.7 to 13.3 cents per point (CPP)** in value. To put that in context: most points are considered "good" redemptions at 1.5–2 CPP. This redemption is 4 to 9 times that benchmark. This is what a true sweet spot looks like. ### Why the Gap Exists Virgin Atlantic prices its ANA partner awards using a **fixed award chart** — a relic of the old loyalty program era when airlines published static pricing tables rather than dynamic, revenue-based pricing. ANA's own Mileage Club program charges 75,000–90,000 miles for the same route. Virgin Atlantic's chart prices it at 90,000, but — and here's the critical part — **with zero fuel surcharges on partner-operated flights**. What you see is what you pay. The result is one of the most compelling premium cabin redemptions in all of loyalty programs. The ChooseFI community's founding principle is that every dollar has a job. When 90,000 transferable points can do the job of $12,000 in cash, that's not just travel rewards — that's an asymmetric opportunity you'd be leaving on the table.

One of the highest cents-per-mile redemptions in all of travel rewards

Here's the aha moment: Virgin Atlantic is selling you access to ANA's inventory at a price ANA itself doesn't offer domestically in the same way. That's the inefficiency. And it's hiding in plain sight.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club maintains a fixed award chart for partner flights. This is increasingly rare in a world where airlines have moved to dynamic, revenue-linked pricing. Because the chart is fixed, Virgin Atlantic charges 90,000 miles for ANA business class between North America and Japan — regardless of whether that seat would cost $6,000 or $12,000 in cash on the day you're flying.

When cash prices spike (holiday season, cherry blossom season, Golden Week), your points cost stays the same. That's not the case when you book directly through ANA Mileage Club, where pricing can vary, or through programs that have adopted dynamic pricing altogether.

This detail alone makes or breaks the redemption. Virgin Atlantic levies high fuel surcharges on its own metal (Virgin-operated flights). Book a Virgin Atlantic-operated long-haul in business class and you might pay $500–$800 in fees on top of your miles.

But when you book partner-operated flights through Virgin Atlantic — specifically ANA — those surcharges drop to zero. You pay government taxes only, typically $50–$100 on a trans-Pacific itinerary. That's it. No fuel surcharge games.

This redemption is accessible because Virgin Atlantic Flying Club accepts transfers from the two most popular transferable points currencies in the ChooseFI ecosystem:

All transfers are instant. This matters because ANA business class availability on partner programs is scarce, and when you find a seat, you need to move fast. You cannot afford to wait 3–5 days for points to post.

Here's a non-obvious but critical piece of tradecraft: you do not search for ANA award availability on Virgin Atlantic's website. Virgin Atlantic's search engine is limited for partner award space. Instead, you search on United.com, because United and ANA are both Star Alliance members and United shows ANA partner award availability accurately in its search results.

Find the space on United.com, confirm the flight numbers and dates, then call or use the online booking tool at flyingclub.virginatlantic.com to complete the booking.

Virgin Atlantic miles expire after 36 months of account inactivity. This means as long as you earn or redeem even one mile every three years, your balance stays alive. Keep that in mind as you accumulate — a small card transaction through the program every couple of years is all it takes to protect a hard-earned balance.

Once you have candidate flights from United.com, go to flyingclub.virginatlantic.com and attempt to search the same flights. Availability is sometimes different between partner search engines, so confirm that Virgin Atlantic can see and price the space before you transfer anything.

Airlines partner with each other through alliances and bilateral agreements, allowing their frequent flyer programs to book seats on each other's flights. The pricing inefficiency occurs when Partner A prices Partner B's premium cabin at a different rate than Partner B charges through its own program. Virgin Atlantic maintains a fixed partner award chart that prices ANA business class at 90,000 miles regardless of demand or seasonality. ANA's own dynamic pricing can push award costs significantly higher during peak periods. This arbitrage between partner pricing and the operating airline's own program is the foundation of most airline travel rewards sweet spots.

Let's make this concrete. You and your partner are planning a trip to Japan. You've been dreaming about it for years — Tokyo, Kyoto, the food, the culture. You want to arrive rested and ready, not wrecked from 14 hours in economy.

By the time you land, you've slept in a proper bed, eaten a multi-course meal, and — critically — you're ready to actually enjoy Japan from day one rather than spending two days recovering from economy class.

Two passengers, one-way: 180,000 Virgin Atlantic miles. That's not an abstraction — that's a real number that changes the calculus of what's possible on a FI timeline.

Virgin Atlantic miles expire after 36 months of account inactivity. This redemption is rated year-round, but ANA's award space to Japan tightens dramatically during cherry blossom season (late March–April), Golden Week (late April–early May), and December holidays. For the best combination of availability and experience, consider September–November or January–February travel.

The most efficient path to 90,000 Virgin Atlantic miles is through Chase Ultimate Rewards (Chase Sapphire Preferred earns 3x on dining and travel; Chase Sapphire Reserve earns 3x on travel and dining) or Amex Membership Rewards (Amex Platinum earns 5x on flights booked directly with airlines). Both transfer 1:1 to Virgin Atlantic instantly.

This redemption is built for the couple or solo traveler who has been building a transferable points balance and is ready to make Japan the centerpiece of a bucket-list trip. If you've been diligently earning Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards and you want to experience what a truly premium long-haul flight feels like — without paying $8,000–$12,000 out of pocket — this is your redemption.

It's particularly well-suited to the FI-minded traveler who values experience over stuff. You're not flying business class because you can't manage without it. You're flying it because 90,000 points delivering $8,000–$12,000 in value is one of the most efficient uses of a points balance available anywhere in loyalty programs today.

For the ChooseFI traveler who has optimized their earning strategy and is ready to deploy a meaningful points balance on a once-in-a-decade trip, this is one of the most compelling redemptions on the board.

## Why This Redemption Is Rated Moderate This isn't a beginner redemption, but it's absolutely within reach for someone who understands the basics of transferable points programs. Here's what makes it moderate rather than easy — and how to handle each challenge. ### Challenge 1: Finding Available Award Space ANA business class partner award seats are genuinely scarce. ANA doesn't release large blocks of partner availability, and what they do release on prime routes like JFK–NRT goes quickly. This is the single biggest obstacle. **The fix:** Search at exactly 331 days out, use United.com for the most accurate availability search, and have flexibility in your travel dates by at least one week in either direction. ### Challenge 2: The Multi-Program Booking Process You're searching on one airline's website (United), transferring points from a bank program (Chase/Amex) to a third airline's loyalty program (Virgin Atlantic), and then booking through that third airline's portal. It's a three-step process across three platforms. **The fix:** Follow the step-by-step process above methodically. Don't rush. Confirm availability before touching your points. ### Challenge 3: Points Accumulation 90,000 miles is a meaningful balance — but it's achievable. Chase Sapphire Reserve's welcome bonus alone can get you most of the way there. This earns a 4 out of 5 on the "Easy to Earn" scale for good reason. ### The Bottom Line If you've successfully transferred points and booked an award before, you can do this. The learning curve is real but short. The reward — flying ANA "The Room" over the Pacific for $60 in fees — makes every minute of research worthwhile.

#8953. What Does Dark Green Poop Mean? Causes, Diet, and When to See a Doctor

Bum nuggets typically sport a classic brown, so glancing back into the loo and spying on greenish-colored poop can throw you for a loop.

Most of the time, green poop reflects a leafy diet or your body’s unique way of breaking things down. But if the green becomes a recurring (fecal) matter, it might be something else.

Continue reading to learn more about poop color, its meaning, and when it’s time to make an appointment with a healthcare provider.

Spotting green or another unexpected color in the toilet can be startling, but it’s more common than you might think. From dietary influences to your body’s digestion speed, several factors can change poop from earthy tones to other shades. Let’s check some out.

Are you chowing down on lots of green leafy veggies like spinach, kale, or broccoli? These foods are high in chlorophyll, which can dye your doodles green. Chlorophyll doesn’t always break down entirely before reaching your intestines, meaning it passes through your system and colors your stool green.

Have you ever had a St. Paddy’s Day-themed milkshake or a brightly colored cake? Artificial colors in foods and drinks can change poop from brown to green. It’s not magic! It’s just the dye in green food passing through your gut unchanged.

When your digestive system processes food too rapidly, it doesn’t allow for the full breakdown of bile, a yellow-green fluid that aids digestion. This often results in a greenish stool, especially during fast-moving episodes of diarrhea.

Have you recently been taking antibiotics? These meds can reset your gut’s bacterial crew. Since these tiny critters play a big part in the shade of your stool, introducing antibiotics might cause green poop sometimes.

If you’ve had certain medical treatments, it can affect digestion and cause bright green poop. One example is graft-versus-host disease, which may occur with bone marrow transplants. This tricky condition can bring about less-than-welcome guests, like diarrhea and green stool. It’s a clear signal from your body that things are out of sync.

Some uninvited microscopic guests like Salmonella bacteria, the water-loving mini parasite Giardia, and norovirus can also be a reason for your poop turning green. These critters can hustle your digestion at an unnaturally quick pace, turning your stool green as they disrupt your gut’s usual rhythm.

Babies can surprise you with a whole crayon box of poop colors, and green is definitely in the mix.

For infants, green stool might stem from the same factors as adults, like dietary changes. This includes adjustments when they start eating solids or changes in a parent’s diet if chestfeeding.

Another harmless cause could be ingesting a small amount of amniotic fluid in the womb. So, if you notice your little one sporting some spring grass-colored diapers, it’s usually no biggie.

If the green theme park in your toilet isn’t closing down, or if it’s accompanied by other symptoms like severe stomach pain, nausea, or diarrhea, it might be time to call in the pros. Persistent changes in stool color may signal underlying health issues that need medical attention.

Dark green poop can result from eating lots of leafy greens or foods with green coloring. However, it can also indicate that food travels quickly through the digestive system.

While liver issues can change stool color, they usually turn it pale or dark, not green. If you’re worried about liver health, look for pale or clay-colored stools instead.

If you haven’t been on a kale-eating spree, dark green poop might be from iron supplements or constipation remedies, which can also give poop a greenish tint.

Dark poop could be a sign of your diet or medications. However, if it’s black and tar-like, it might mean bleeding in your upper gastrointestinal tract. In that case, chatting with a healthcare professional is a must.

While green poop can def throw you through a loop, it’s usually not a sign of anything serious. It’s often your body’s way of dealing with what you eat or how fast you digest. So, unless it’s paired with other worrying symptoms, there’s probably no need to panic.

Last medically reviewed on August 2, 2024

#8952. Nike Tuned Air "a huge stride forward" in air-filled trainer design says innovation lead

Sportswear brand Nike has unveiled the 3D-printed air bags that will be used for its next generation of air-filled trainers. In this interview, the brand’s chief innovation, design & product officer Phil McCartney explains why it is a technological and performance advance.

“I see it personally as a revolution, not an evolution,” McCartney told Dezeen from the LeBron James Innovation Center in Oregon. “It’s a huge stride forward.”

Tuned Air was designed to give Nike much greater control of how air is used within the midsole to provide cushioning and support. Using a combination of proprietary 3D printing and “selective lamination” allows Nike to create midsoles that perform in different ways under different parts of the foot.

Informed by the raised vibrant colours on magazine covers, the airbag is built up from layers of ink.

“We can engineer the structure and tune the structure in the heel differently to the forefoot,” said McCartney.

“We can also tune the height, so you can have a variety of different heights, and we can tune the structure inside.”

Nike unveiled the technology and concept images for a running shoe today, and is planning for the first Nike Tuned Air trainer to be launched next year.

The trainers will be the first in what Nike sees as a third major generation of its air-filled shoes, since Nike CEO Phil Knight worked with inventor Frank Rudy to use a cushioning system filled with gas in the late 1970s.

Following the Nike Air Tailwind in 1978, Nike developed Air Max in the 1980s and Air Zoom in the 1990s.

“At its core, Air, for 50 years, has been this magical combination of lightweight, cushioned and resilient – it doesn’t break down over time,” said McCartney. “That’s why from day one when Phil [Knight] struck the deal with Frank Rudy, we’ve been so committed to it – it just delivers a really unique benefit.”

“If Max Air is about maximal cushioning and impact protection, Zoom Air is more about responsiveness and snappiness,” he continued. “Tuned Air, because of this proprietary ink and selective lamination process, allows us to literally tune the sensation within the airbag, which enables us to sort of move free from the constraints of typical geometry and shape.”

According to McCartney, this change in how the airbags are manufactured opens up possibilities, especially in customisation.

“It is the first step in exploring all the different places that this will go,” said McCartney. “The capability and what we’re able to do with this proprietary ink and the selective lamination allows us to really unlock the real potential of air.”

“It also creates this canvas for all the design explorations that we’ve always wanted to do, but the limitations of the manufacturing process didn’t allow,” he continued.

“So now the handcuffs are off in terms of it being a canvas – what expressions do we want to explore? What different visuals, geometries, and different ways to articulate the benefit can we explore? We’re looking at all of that. “

While the air-filled midsole has been manufactured, the trainer is still in development. However, McCartney expects the shoe to look close to the concept render that was revealed today.

“There’ll be a few modifications,” he said. “Knowing where the design is going to go. It’s pretty representative as an illustration, but it isn’t the final design.” He noted that the final air bag design will be close to the prototype.

“What we’re exploring now is how do we take the idea of lightweight cushioning and this idea of tuned [and find] what that looks like in an expression and an experience on the upper.”

One key design element that will feature in the commercial release next year will be the full-length, visible air bag, which McCartney said is an “important part of the design and important part of this platform”.

The midsoles are the latest innovation in Nike’s exploration of using air within footwear and apparel. While it has made millions of shoes containing air, it has also recently unveiled the inflating Air Milano Jacket at 2026 Winter Olympics and its Radical AirFlow t-shirts that counterintuitively use more material to make a wearer cooler.

In all the areas of innovation that McCartney oversees at Nike, air is where he sees the most potential.

“There’s a number of areas, but if I had to pick one, I think that [air] is the platform that intrigues us most, that drives our creativity the most, that also translates into the biggest athlete benefit. And I mean athlete in the broadest sense of the term – if you’ve got a body, you’re an athlete.”

“We’re really intrigued and fascinated by the notion of being able to harness what’s all around us to further performance,” said McCartney. “That started in footwear, obviously. This is the next revolution.”

#8950. neri oxman’s material ecology imagines a future where buildings grow like living organisms

through two decades of research at the intersection of biology, computation, and fabrication, the designer proposes a new relationship between human invention and the intelligence of nature.

In her book Mediated Matter: Design and Invention in the New Biological Age, multidisciplinary designer Neri Oxman explores how biology, computation, and digital fabrication could reshape the way humans make and build. Drawing on two decades of research developed through her former practice, The Mediated Matter Group at the MIT Media Lab, the 612-page monograph introduces Material Ecology, an approach to design that positions nature as an active participant in the creation of materials, objects, and architecture.

The publication arrives at a moment when the consequences of human construction are difficult to ignore. Around 2020, the mass of human-made materials surpassed the total biomass of living organisms on Earth, according to research published in Nature. This imbalance brings into focus one of the central propositions of Oxman’s work, moving beyond the extraction and consumption of natural resources to explore ways of creating structures that actively contribute to the ecosystems they inhabit.

The research behind Material Ecology took shape within The Mediated Matter Group, which Oxman founded and directed at the MIT Media Lab between 2010 and 2020. Working across architecture, engineering, synthetic biology, and digital fabrication, the group developed technologies that allowed biological processes and computational systems to operate together.

Among its best-known experiments is the Silk Pavilion, an architectural structure produced through the collaboration of robotic fabrication and 6,500 live silkworms. The project explored how their natural spinning behavior of the insects could participate in the construction of an architectural form. By controlling the distribution of fibers through light and heat, the researchers investigated how biological activity could complement robotic precision.

Other experiments approached material production through different biological and chemical processes. Glass explored the possibilities of 3D printing molten glass at furnace temperatures, creating structures with varying geometries and optical properties. Synthetic Apiary investigated the relationship between architecture and pollinators through an environment designed around the needs of bees. With Aguahoja, the group developed water-based bioplastics using materials including apple skins and shrimp shells. The structures were designed to respond to environmental conditions and eventually dissolve back into their constituent elements.

Buildings are usually designed to withstand changes in their surroundings. Oxman questions this separation between architecture and the environment, considering how building materials might react to temperature, moisture, and light, and how biological processes could become part of their function. She uses three terms to describe this possibility: atoms, bits, and genes. Atoms refer to physical matter, bits to computational intelligence, and genes to biological growth. Their combination forms the basis for materials that bring together the structural qualities of standard building components with the capacity for change.

The designer uses the example of a brick to show how atoms, bits, and genes might come together in a single building material. It would combine physical matter with computational intelligence and the capacity for biological growth, allowing the brick to respond to changes and interact with living processes.

The book organizes its exploration of Material Ecology around six material systems: Biopolymers, Organic Comb, Natural Fibers, Vitreous Solids, Programmable Matter, and Pigments. Each chapter follows four interconnected principles: Position, Process, Product, and Praxis, examining why a material matters, how it can be manipulated, what can be produced from it, and what broader changes its application might enable. Oxman outlines a series of principles that challenge established assumptions about design and production. Nature becomes a co-client, growth takes precedence over assembly, systems become more important than isolated objects and biological differences are valued over industrial repetition.

Oxman proposes a cross-species perspective in which plants, animals, and other organisms are considered both contributors to and beneficiaries of designed environments, shifting the designer’s responsibility beyond the immediate needs of a human client. The principle of decay over disposal extends this argument into the entire lifespan of an object. Materials are understood as temporarily diverted from their ecological contexts. Once obsolete, they should be able to return to their environments and support new growth.

In Mediated Matter, Oxman gathers these investigations into an argument for moving beyond the opposition between protecting nature and advancing human technology. Her proposition is that the two might become mutually reinforcing, with design acting as the mediator between biological systems and human invention. Her vision is neither a return to an untouched natural world nor a future in which technology becomes more efficient. It imagines a different kind of coexistence, where the boundaries between the grown and the made become difficult to distinguish.

#8949. Photos reveal scale of Trump’s White House ballroom, drawing criticism

Earlier this month, Trump’s White House ballroom and military bunker laid its final structural steel beam, with politicians and critics weighing in on the scale of the project.

Recently taken images of the extension, which show the structure with massive concrete shear walls, steel beams, and columns, along with a partially enclosed roof structure, have drawn attention to the scale of the building.

No sign of its planned neoclassical ornamentation has yet been implemented.

Officially called the East Wing Modernization Project, the structure dwarfs the Executive Residence and West Wing.

Trump announced the laying of the last steel beam in the superstructure on 4 November, the day after the national midterm elections.

“This is a special structure,” Trump said on a tour on 4 November, according to NBC News. “It’s going to be not only one of the biggest, but it’ll be the most beautiful ballroom, I think, anywhere in the world, and they’ve been trying to get it for 150 years.”

It says everything about Donald Trump that his gilded ballroom dwarfs the size of the People's House—and it says everything about the American people that they repudiated him loudly and clearly last Tuesday. pic.twitter.com/ou23LpAes8

Since then, there has been a renewed wave of criticism online over the project, ranging from outrage to humour.

Former senator and presidential candidate Hillary Clinton wrote on X (formerly Twitter), commenting on the size of the structure and noting the midterm election’s “repudiation” of Trump.

“It says everything about Donald Trump that his gilded ballroom dwarfs the size of the People’s House—and it says everything about the American people that they repudiated him loudly and clearly last Tuesday,” wrote Clinton.

Congressman Jim Clyburn took a similar stance in a statement on Facebook, noting that the ballroom was “much bigger” than the rest of the White House.

Architecture critic Kate Wagner took a more humorous approach, noting that the ballroom is not neoclassical in construction. Wagner compared it to a Ramada Inn, a chain of hotels in the US, that they will “glue pediments to”.

“[It’s] an outcome designed in a lab to make everyone angry. possibly the most trump building ever built,” wrote Wagner on X.com.

The ballroom has been controversial since Trump demolished the White House’s West Wing in October 2025. The National Capital Planning Commission approved the project in April.

It has faced legal challenges, with US District Judge Leon issuing a stay in response to a lawsuit led by the National Trust for Historic Preservation.

the fact that trump's ballroom is clearly not neoclassical in any way shape or form is possibly the funniest moment in architectural history

In August, the Supreme Court allowed the project to continue, though the dissenting opinion said it was “likely unlawful”.

Despite the legal challenges, construction has continued, with Trump’s team leaning on the national security aspects of the underground bunker.

The administration has also floated plans to add a screening facility at Sherman Park – a small park to the southwest of the White House. Trump also installed a paved helipad on the White House lawn.

#8947. Against Program: The Productive Ambiguity of Contemporary Architecture

This article is part of our new Opinion section, a format for argument-driven essays on critical questions shaping our field.

This article is part of our new Opinion section, a format for argument-driven essays on critical questions shaping our field.

In 2022, Tokyo's Nakagin Capsule Tower was demolished, bringing an end to one of modern architecture's most recognizable experiments in adaptability. Designed by Kisho Kurokawa and completed in 1972, the building consisted of 140 prefabricated capsules attached to two concrete cores. Its architectural proposition was radical: individual capsules could be replaced as needs evolved, allowing the building to renew itself without dismantling its principal structure. Yet over five decades, the proposed replacement system was never realized. Despite various preservation efforts, deteriorating building services and difficulties in collective decision-making eventually led to its demolition.

#8946. Dezeen Awards 2026 design project of the year winner named

The wayfinding scheme for London‘s V&A East Storehouse has won Dezeen Awards 2026 design project of the year following the announcement of all 16 design category winners at a party in London.

The 16 winners awarded in Dezeen’s annual awards programme include designs by Laurids Gallée and John Tree, as well as Foster + Partners and Kettal.

Fieldwork Facility’s graphic identity for the V&A East Storehouse experience won the design project of the year award and was also named graphic design of the year.

V&A East Storehouse by Fieldwork Facility

The master jury cited the project as a “sophisticated wayfinding scheme that demonstrates how signage can do far more than direct: it can define identity, shape experience and establish a sense of place”.

The judges praised the design for its “clarity, confidence and restraint, seamlessly guiding visitors through the V&A East Storehouse while adding to the character of the building”.

V&A East Storehouse was up against designs that included a constellation of gloopy-looking polished resin lights, an electric cargo bike with the carrying capacity of a small van and a low-carbon, concrete-like floor tile strengthened by bacteria.

Read more about all the winning design projects below:

Design project of the year and graphic design of the year: V&A East Storehouse by Fieldwork Facility

Design studio Fieldwork Facility was challenged with navigating visitors to the V&A’s storage vault, including 250,000 historic art, craft and design objects – especially a younger, more diverse crowd who might normally feel excluded from museums.

This fun and informative signage and wayfinding perfectly embraces the changing nature of the V&A East Storehouse

The Hackney design studio looked to an unexpected source of inspiration when creating wayfinding for London’s V&A East Storehouse: Gen-Z apps and services.

“This fun and informative signage and wayfinding perfectly embraces the changing nature of the V&A East Storehouse,” said the master jury.

“As the displays change, the signage, captions and general wayfinding can be updated efficiently, embracing the adaptability and lack of formality of the museum.”

Furniture design of the year: Dado Series by Allen Kaufmann Objects

Berlin studio Allen Kaufmann Architekten won furniture design of the year for its Dado series of tables and shelves.

What is simple in appearance is underscored with a well-resolved and detailed construction made from a monomaterial

The practice adapted a traditional woodworking joint to create a flat-pack range that can be assembled completely without tools nor glue, screws, brackets or other fasteners.

“What is simple in appearance is underscored with a well-resolved and detailed construction made from a monomaterial,” the judges said. “The shelving is satisfying to assemble and demonstrates everything furniture needs to be, and no more.”

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Seating design of the year: Kino by Pablo Castillo Design

Barcelona-based designer Pablo Castillo won seating design of the year for Kino, a cantilevered 3D-printed chair for Decibel.

Modern shapes meet zero-waste manufacturing; surely the future

The designer’s aim was to create a recognisable chair silhouette, while also responding to the specificities of the 3D printing process.

Its entire form is printed from PLA, the most common bioplastic, although the material is reinforced with cellulose plant fibres. This increases its strength, enabling the cantilevered seat.

“The 3D printing of furniture is becoming more refined and this is a strong example of that,” said the master jury.

“The mono-material construction is sophisticated and has a strong aesthetic profile,” they continued. “Modern shapes meet zero-waste manufacturing; surely the future.”

Collectible design of the year: Lima Charlie by Studio Laurids Gallée

Austrian designer Laurids Gallée won collectible design of the year for Lima Charlie, a series of five colourful, sculptural lamps.

Mesmerising, intriguing and evocative, these lights are truly original and demonstrate a high level of care in their meticulous craftsmanship

The lighting collection comprises five hand-cast resin light works and machined aluminium pieces.

First, the designer used digital processes to determine each composition. Then, casting solid blocks of the material before colouring, cutting and sculpting them into shape. Each piece was meticulously sanded and polished to arrive at the desired smooth surface.

“Mesmerising, intriguing and evocative, these lights are truly original and demonstrate a high level of care in their meticulous craftsmanship,” praised the judges. “Beautiful treasures to enhance any space.”

Bespoke design of the year: Real Time Schiphol People’s Clock by Maarten Baas

Dutch designer Maarten Baas won bespoke design of the year for The People’s Clock, a choreographed representation of the passage of time at Amsterdam’s Schiphol Airport.

It was an ambitious undertaking to make the piece, which celebrates and gives ownership to the airport workers

Baas recruited 1,000 participants – the majority being airport employees – to form the hands of The People’s Clock and move in sync, forming the hour and minute hands. The second hand comprises a single person running a lap of the circular perimeter each minute.

“This timepiece in Amsterdam’s busy airport momentarily takes users away from the efficient functionality of the space by providing a reference to the time in a more playful and poetic way,” said the master jury.

“It was an ambitious undertaking to make the piece, which celebrates and gives ownership to the airport workers.”

Lighting design of the year: Hoop Table Lamp by John Tree for Vaarnii

Designer John Tree won lighting design of the year for the Hoop Table Lamp for Finnish brand Vaarni.

There is a confidence in the minimal use of materials and a cuteness in the ensuing form

The monolithic light combines a block of solid pine wood – synonymous with the Finnish brand’s designs – with a hooped shade of thin pine veneer, sourced from a sustainably managed forest.

“We were all drawn to the simple and characterful gestures of this table lamp, which embraces warmth from a common timber,” the judges said.

“There is a confidence in the minimal use of materials and a cuteness in the ensuing form.”

Architectural lighting design of the year: Cologne Cathedral by Licht Kunst Licht

Lighting design studio Licht Kunst Licht won architectural lighting design of the year for its illumination of Cologne Cathedral’s historic facade.

This well-considered lighting scheme successfully highlights Cologne’s monumental cathedral as a jewel on the night skyline

The lighting scheme used more than 700 surface-mounted LED luminaires to transform nighttime views of the world’s tallest cathedral without drilling a single hole in its delicate stonework.

“This well-considered lighting scheme successfully highlights Cologne’s monumental cathedral as a jewel on the night skyline,” the judges praised.

“The light sources are subtly integrated and have managed to reduce energy consumption while creating maximum impact for this city landmark,” they added.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Surface design of the year: Basic Third by Pretty Plastic

Dutch manufacturer Pretty Plastic won surface design of the year for its Basic Third tiles.

There is an inherent beauty and honesty to the product, adding texture and depth to the architecture

The cladding material was developed by the Pretty Plastic company, started by architecture studios Overtreders W and Bureau SLA.

The tiles, which were made from 30,987 kilograms of post-consumer plastic waste, have been applied as cladding for Plus Ultra III, the first timber laboratory building in the Netherlands.

“Pretty Plastics has chosen to work with the worst kind of plastic – PVC – and found a way to repurpose the material into tiles,” said the judges.

“The material is already fire-compliant and UV stable, making it a worthy contender for the cladding of buildings,” they continued. “There is an inherent beauty and honesty to the product, adding texture and depth to the architecture.”

Looking ahead, the judges said “its impact will be proven by how easy it is to scale.”

Textile design of the year: Bianni Wool Paper by Arudeko

Mexican design studio won textile design of the year for Bianni, a paper-like material made from colourful waste wool.

With so much wool waste in the world, this new material adds value to the waste

Sourced from the off-cuts of handmade carpets and cushions crafted by local weaving communities in Teotitlán del Valle, Mexico, Arudeko saw the potential to use the surplus material and save it from being discarded.

Bianni can be sculpted into everything from lampshades to room dividers.

“With so much wool waste in the world, this new material adds value to the waste,” the judges commended.

“Furthermore, the processing provides employment to skilled locals, the outcome being an interesting and beautiful paper alternative to be applied to other products,” they said. “There is much potential for further exploration across the world.”

Workplace design of the year: Area by Foster + Partners and Kettal

Foster + Partners and Kettal won workplace design of the year for their modular Area table system.

There is an appealing monumentalism to this office desk and a tactility in the simplicity and richness of the material composition

Designed to be durable and adaptable, Area combines aluminium columns, a panoply of tabletop options and concealed power. The aluminium columns anchor the design, serving as both structural support and discreet container for power cables and electrical components.

“There is an appealing monumentalism to this office desk and a tactility in the simplicity and richness of the material composition,” said the judges.

“There are sophisticated elements and thoughtful hidden details for integrating technology into an otherwise minimalist design,” they continued.

Product design (consumer design) of the year: Pedal 4 by Minimal

British start-up Minimal won product design (consumer design) of the year for Pedal 4, an electric cargo bike with the carrying capacity of a small van.

A smart new vehicle typology that addresses the challenges of inner city deliveries

The four-wheeled, pedal-assist cargo vehicle was built to take up less room on the roads and evade traffic even on London’s crowded and complex streets. It is now operating in London with delivery companies Royal Mail and Evri.

“A smart new vehicle typology that addresses the challenges of inner city deliveries,” praised the judges.

“This is a great ‘last mile’ replacement for large polluting vans. The slender design manoeuvres easily in city streets while the electric motor emits no noxious pollutants,” they continued.

“The vehicles’ local assembly also allows it to be easily repaired.”

Product design (health, wellbeing and wearables) of the year: CurifyLabs PharmaPrinter Aurum by Studio Aslak Siimes

Industrial design firm Studio Aslak Siimes and Finnish startup CurifyLabs won product design (health, wellbeing and wearables) of the year for pharmaceutical compounding system, PharmaPrinter Aurum.

It’s refreshing to see something so functional having also been aesthetically considered

The system is designed to improve the process of creating patient-specific medicine, born from the realisation that almost 30 per cent of all medication requires personalisation rather than being mass-manufactured, according to studio founder Aslak Siimes.

“This device offers a real innovation in precision healthcare and decentralises the production of pills,” the judges said. “Precise medical doses are prepared bespoke for each customer, reducing waste and eliminating human error.”

“Furthermore, it’s refreshing to see something so functional having also been aesthetically considered,” they added.

Product design (bathroom) of the year: Dekoda by Kohler Health

Kohler Health won product design (bathroom) of the year for Dekoda, a health tracker specifically for the toilet.

This is an innovative, early-diagnostic device for ongoing monitoring of health conditions

Designed to be discreet and intuitive, the tracker clips to the side of the toilet bowl to give insights on gut health and hydration levels, and to detect the presence of blood.

“This is an innovative, early-diagnostic device for ongoing monitoring of health conditions,” the judges said. “The design of the device is discreet and visually passive, making it suitable for its function in the bathroom.”

Installation design of the year: Einder for USB002 Tour by Boris Acket and Fred Again

Visual artist Boris Acket won installation design of the year for Einder, which featured as the standout show design for DJ Fred again..’s USB002 Tour.

This lightweight and flexible installation uses minimum material to maximum effect, making it evocative while sustainable. More please!

The installation features a large suspended sheet of fabric which floats above the audience like a transparent, breathing roof.

Throughout the concert, the sculpture wafts and moves across the audience, creating smaller and larger spaces, static spatial gestures, storms, and water surfaces.

The judges summed up the project as “stunning, emotive, immersive, dynamic, simple”.

“This lightweight and flexible installation uses minimum material to maximum effect, making it evocative while sustainable. More please!”

Sustainable design of the year: Datecrete by Datecrete Studio

Architect Sara Abu Farha and engineer Khaled Shalka won sustainable design of the year for Datecrete, a concrete-style material developed by Abu Farha and Shalka formed from crushed dates.

This is a necessary regional innovation, repurposing an abundant waste material (date pits) into a local construction material, and providing a welcome alternative to concrete

The project aims to demonstrate how the abundant regional byproduct can become part of an architectural material language. Patent-pending, Datecrete can be produced as floor and wall tiles, cladding, furniture, lighting elements and smaller design objects.

“This is a necessary regional innovation, repurposing an abundant waste material (date pits) into a local construction material, and providing a welcome alternative to concrete,” said the master jury.

“The processing of the pits is decentralised, so it has the potential to scale in communities across the date-growing region.”

Material innovation of the year: Mimmik Tile by Front

Dutch sustainability platform Front and biotechnology company Biomason won material innovation of the year for Mimmik, a low-carbon, concrete-like floor tile strengthened by bacteria.

This tile design is genuinely pushing innovation forward in its creation; collaborating with bacteria as a sustainable alternative to concrete

Front believes Mimmik is the first bacteria-grown tile to be industrially produced, making a sustainable technology available to a wide market of specifiers looking to reduce the carbon footprint of their commercial projects.

“This tile design is genuinely pushing innovation forward in its creation; collaborating with bacteria as a sustainable alternative to concrete,” praised the judges.

“As such, the embodied carbon is greatly reduced,” they noted. “The production is scalable and could shift the dial in the future production of tiles and paving.”

#8944. How to Calculate Your Rising and Moon Sign: A Beginner’s Guide

The sun sign is the *it girlie* of the “big three” elements in astrology.

But do you know about your moon sign and rising sign?

We chatted with an astrologer to understand what they are and how to calculate them.

According to Olga Verkhotina — astrologer and personal coach — the big three in astrology are your three most significant chart elements:

“While a natal chart contains so many more intricate details beyond just three elements, the big three is a way to determine the main highlights that make up your personality and overall temperament,” Verkhotina says.

Verkhotina explains that a rising sign is the zodiac sign that falls at the beginning of your First House — basically, the beginning of your natal chart.

“The First House in astrology is associated with a person’s identity, individual activity, even their appearance, and the sign that houses that theme gives its characteristics,” she says.

“Knowing your rising sign describes the way others may perceive you, the way your behavior comes across, as well as how you approach new situations in life.”

You’ll need: date, time and place of birth.

“Knowing the accurate time is important here because even 10 minutes can make a difference in the sign,” Verkhotina explains.

“Once you have the data, you can trust astrology software to calculate it for you. There are a lot of natal chart calculators online, so you can just search ‘rising sign calculator,'” Verkhotina says.

Pro tip: Verkhotina suggests reading horoscopes from your rising sign instead of your sun sign, saying it will likely give more personalized insights on which areas of your life might be impacted by current cosmic events.

“A moon sign describes the position of the moon on the zodiac wheel at the moment of your birth,” Verkhotina says.

She explains that the moon in astrology symbolizes:

“The moon sign helps you better understand how these themes demonstrate themselves in your life,” Verkhotina says.

Unlike the rising sign, you don’t have to have the precise time of birth to know your moon sign, although Verkhotina says it’s still recommended.

You can also use an online calculator to find your moon sign or refer to the ephemeris — a table showing the daily positions of planets.

Verkhotina describes the sun sign as the most important planet in your chart.

“It’s the center of your vitality, your ego, consciousness, and individuality at its core. That’s why it’s the most commonly known element in astrology,” she says.

It represents the zodiac sign the sun was in at the time of your birth, which Verkhotina says gives your individuality certain qualities associated with its specific sign.

“It’s important to understand that although the sun is a huge element in astrology, it doesn’t cover the nuances of one’s character,” Verkhotina explains.

Instead, she says it just represents overall traits.

Verkhotina adds that the specifics of your character are covered in the rest of your astrological chart. “This is why sometimes no two leos are the same,” she says.

This one is easy peasy — you don’t have to have your time or place of birth.

“The sun cycle is very similar every year, so you can look it up by the date, month and year of your birth. Each sign corresponds to a calendar date that year,” Verkhotina says.

Here’s each astro sign, in a nutshell, according to Verkhotina.

Your sun sign is important, but your moon and rising signs add extra details.

Your rising sign reflects your identity and how others see you, while your moon sign reveals your emotions and behavior.

To find these signs, you can use online birth chart calculators. Just make sure you have your birth date and time handy for accurate results.

#8943. vhils and marcelo cidade shroud historic são paulo building in a shimmering silver skin

using silver thermal sheets and cornstarch paste, the artists transform an historic building into a study of architecture and urban memory.

Portuguese artist Vhils (Alexandre Farto) and Brazilian artist Marcelo Cidade have wrapped the facade of an old building in São Paulo with reflective silver thermal sheets. Titled 2878, after its address on Rua Cardeal Arcoverde in the Pinheiros neighborhood, the intervention gives the historic structure a metallic new appearance. Its original architectural features are expressed beneath the covering, while the silver surface catches the changing light of the street.

The artists have applied individual sheets of thermal material directly to the facade using a simple adhesive made from cornstarch. The lightweight covering follows the contours of the existing architecture, picking out its openings and decorative details. Depending on the angle of the sunlight, the building appears to glow against its surroundings or reflect them back in fragmented patches. The public artwork plays with this shifting visibility to draw attention to an address that would have otherwise likely blended into the streetscape.

The building itself has an interesting past. Records dating back to 1945 identify the property as the site of a tuberculosis dispensary operated by São Paulo’s public health authorities. A government decree from 1953 further documents its use for the Pinheiros dispensary, while more recent records identify it as a former home of SUCEN, the state’s agency for controlling endemic diseases.

The structure has remained on the same street for decades, and has passed through different uses as the neighborhood has changed around it. By temporarily concealing its original surfaces, Vhils and Cidade bring its architecture back into public view. Their intervention considers how familiar buildings can gradually fade from a city’s collective awareness, even while continuing to occupy a prominent place in the urban landscape.

The project marks the first collaboration between the two artists, whose practices have long engaged with the built environment. Vhils is widely recognized for his portraits carved directly into urban walls, where removing layers of plaster and concrete reveals images beneath the surface. Cidade often works with architectural elements and materials drawn from the street, and examines how buildings shape people’s relationships with public space.

The silver sheeting recalls a protective thermal blanket which suggests an attempt to both preserve the building and obscure its original character. This tension is central to the work. The reflective facade can make the architecture unusually conspicuous, while its shifting surface also allows the building to visually dissolve into the city around it.

The installation arrives alongside Vhils’ exhibition ATRITO: Arqueologia do Presente (Friction: Archaeology of the Present), which opened at Galleria Continua in São Paulo on November 14th, 2026. Curated by Ana Carolina Ralston, the exhibition explores the physical traces left by urban transformation.

Among its central works are fourteen corroded metal cubes arranged as a labyrinth, their surfaces marked with fragments of portraits and signage drawn from cities around the world. Vhils has also created a separate large-scale intervention across the gallery’s glass facade.

Outside the gallery, 2878 brings these ideas directly into the neighborhood. The choice of an existing building, along with the inexpensive materials used to cover it, gives the installation an immediate relationship with the street. For a time, the familiar address becomes a reflective landmark, its architectural details newly apparent beneath the silver covering.

the reflective material follows the contours of the building’s original facadesilver thermal sheets are applied using a cornstarch-based adhesivethe facade shifts in appearance as sunlight interacts with the metallic covering

location: Rua Cardeal Arcoverde 2878, Pinheiros, São Paulo, Brazil related exhibition: ATRITO: Arqueologia do Presente gallery: Galleria Continua
